itineraries.title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from the glassworks of Kosta and Orrefors to Astrid Lindgren’s hometown, to Eksjö, and to the island of Visingsö.
itineraries.notes: Go between mid-June and mid-August: Astrid Lindgrens Värld, the childhood home at Näs, Kumlaby Church, and the horse-drawn carriages on Visingsö all operate daily then. You can watch glassblowing from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., daily in Kosta and Tuesday through Sunday in Orrefors.
itineraries.climate: Aim for mid-June to mid-August: in Växjö, average highs range from 20 °C in June to 22.5 °C in July, and most attractions are open daily then. July and August are also the rainiest months: bring a rain jacket, especially since umbrellas are prohibited during performances at Astrid Lindgrens Värld. Avoid winter: the park and the house at Näs are closed, and highs hover around 0 to 2 °C.

visits.text: Before watching glassblowing, it helps to understand what you are seeing. The Swedish Glass Museum, housed in the Smålands museum in Växjö, traces the country’s glassmaking from antiquity to “studio glass,” one-of-a-kind pieces that artists blow in their own studios. The Smålands museum is described as Sweden’s oldest county museum (regional museum). Admission is 150 kronor per adult and free for visitors ages 18 and under. The museum is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Start your road trip in Växjö, the most convenient gateway to the route. You can arrive by train or fly from Stockholm-Bromma: the airport is about ten kilometers northwest of town. Rent your car here, since Kosta is just a 42-minute drive away. The route ends in Jönköping: if you need to return the car in Växjö, Krösatåg regional trains connect the two cities.

practical_info.tip: Your museum ticket also includes admission to the House of Emigrants in central Växjö.

visits.text: The heat hits you as soon as you enter the glassblowing hall at Kosta Glasbruk. Furnaces have been burning in Kosta since 1742, making it Sweden’s oldest glassworks still in operation. Its name combines the first syllables of its two founders’ names, Koskull and Staël von Holstein. About 25 glassblowers work here across five workshops. You can visit the hall daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. for 70 kronor per adult: avoid 11 to 11:45 a.m., when the artisans take their break.

In 1955, Kosta expanded its showroom with a glass-walled wing designed by architect Bruno Mathsson. Look down: the floor is a glass mosaic made at the glassworks. Now the Kosta Art Gallery, the space displays art pieces by Kosta Boda’s designers. Exhibitions change two or three times a year. It is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday until 4 p.m.

Nineveh, Jerusalem, Babylon: the workers’ houses on Stora vägen, Kosta’s main street, bore the names of biblical cities. Built from the mid-18th century onward, these glassworkers’ homes were renovated in 1810 and have changed little since. Kosta’s manor house dates to 1758. Also look for Glashuset, a row of five homes designed by Bruno Mathsson, with insulating double glazing that he had patented. You can walk around the glassworks freely, at no charge.

activities.text: If you want to take home something you have blown yourself, book an introductory glassblowing session at Kosta Glasbruk. An artisan guides you step by step, and sessions start at around 500 kronor for a glass ball. In the evening, ask about hyttsill, an old glassworks tradition. You dine on herring and Småland dishes cooked in the furnaces where glass cools slowly, while watching glassblowers at work.

practical_info.tip: Public hyttsill evenings mainly take place in summer and before Christmas: check the dates on the Kingdom of Crystal website.

activities.text: Drive at walking speed in your own car among the moose at Kosta Safaripark. The park covers 200 hectares of forest, roughly the size of 280 soccer fields. Bison, red deer, and wild boar also roam freely here. Book your visit through the Kingdom of Crystal booking website: prices start at 135 kronor, with free cancellation up to 24 hours in advance.

practical_info.tip: The park is in Kosta itself, at 1 Visentvägen: there is no need to get back on the main road.

visits.text: Orrefors has lost its large glassworks, but not its glassblowers. Founded in 1898, the factory stopped production on July 12, 2013, when its owner moved manufacturing abroad. The Orranäs Glasbruk workshop later fired up furnaces on the site again. Its hall burned down in 2023, and a new octagonal hall was completed the following year. You can watch glassblowing up close Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The Orrefors museum displays the glassworks’ historical collection, from early pieces to recent creations. Before glass, Orrefors depended on iron: ironworks were established here in 1726, and the glassworks later occupied their site. In Hammarsmedjan, the restored forge, you can still hear the heavy hammer that once shaped iron into bars striking. Allow half an hour for the two, then drive to Målerås, 13 minutes away.

A highlight of the route is Målerås, a glassworks saved by its workers. Founded in 1890, it was bought in 1981 by designer Mats Jonasson and his colleagues to keep it running. Its specialty is animal reliefs engraved in crystal. The showroom and store are open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m.

activities.text: Have lunch at Målerås Glasbruk: during the high season, the restaurant has large windows overlooking the glassblowing hall. You can eat while watching molten glass take shape. The neighboring craft center sells ceramics, jewelry, wooden objects, and local products. Then allow 1 hour 36 minutes to drive to Vimmerby.

practical_info.tip: You can also book a session to blow your own piece at Målerås through the Kingdom of Crystal website.

visits.text: Astrid Lindgren was born in 1907 on Näs farm, then on the outskirts of Vimmerby. The Astrid Lindgrens Näs center was built on the very spot where she grew up, a few minutes’ walk from the main square. Its major exhibition is called “Astrid Lindgren and the Power of Stories.” Continue your visit in the gardens. In 2027, the site is open daily from May 21 to September 26.

The bed where Astrid Lindgren was born, the harmonium, a cushion she embroidered: her childhood home at Näs is still furnished as it was when she was a child. The family still owns it, and entry is by guided tour only. The tour lasts about 45 minutes, with visitors standing throughout, and is limited to 12 people ages 8 and up. English tours are also offered from May to September. Book as soon as tickets for 2027 go on sale.

Sit across from Astrid Lindgren on Stora torget, Vimmerby’s main square. Marie-Louise Ekman’s bronze statue, unveiled in 2007, shows her at her typewriter, with an empty chair opposite for visitors. Then head down Storgatan, the main street, which still follows its medieval route, and explore the cobblestone lanes around the square, including Båtsmansbacken. Astrid Lindgren is buried in the family grave in the town cemetery.

If your children could see only one setting at Astrid Lindgrens Värld, the theme park devoted to the writer’s stories, it would be Villa Villekulla. This is the home of Pippi Longstocking, whom Swedes call Pippi Långstrump. According to the park’s 2026 schedule, Pippi performed here six times a day. Bring a raincoat instead of an umbrella, as umbrellas are prohibited during performances.

Katthult was the very first house in the park, which opened in 1981 under the name Sagobyn, “the storybook village.” It is the farm where Emil lives, the mischievous boy French readers knew as Zozo la tornade. It was built at one-third of its actual size, as were all the sets built afterward, putting them on a child’s scale. Emil performed here five times a day in 2026: note the showtimes as soon as you enter, as the park covers 18 hectares.

Here, humor gives way to adventure. Mattis’s Castle provides the setting for Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter, and Cherry Valley for the story of The Brothers Lionheart. In 2026, each of these two settings hosted four shows a day. One of the park’s shows, “The Day of the Battle,” includes frightening scenes and effects. The park recommends it for ages 9 and up: check the program before settling in with young children.

activities.text: Plan your day around the shows at Astrid Lindgrens Värld: the 2026 program included 28 daily performances, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. They are performed in Swedish, so tell the children the stories before you go. In 2026, a one-day ticket in peak season cost 565 kronor per adult and 430 per child, with free admission for children under 3. The park’s stores and restaurants do not accept cash. In 2027, the park is open daily from May 21 to August 22.

practical_info.tip: After August 22, 2027, the park opens only Friday through Sunday until the end of September, then during fall break.

activities.text: The best moment of the day is not always a show. Between performances, let the children try the “Don’t Touch the Ground” trail, where they make their way along without setting foot on the ground. The Tiny Town, the play barn, and the hamlet of Bullerbyn, drawn from another series of books, round out this vast playground. There are plenty of picnic areas: securely close any bags left in your stroller, as the park’s birds help themselves.

practical_info.tip: Dogs are allowed on a short leash, but not inside buildings.

visits.text: In 1856, a fire destroyed half of Eksjö but spared the northern part of its wooden old town. This district, Gamla stan, is lined with wooden houses from the 17th and 18th centuries and has numerous courtyards. Almost the entire old town has protected heritage status. Eksjö has also received the Europa Nostra Award, a European distinction for heritage conservation. In summer, the town museum organizes guided walks.

Eksjö museum tells the story of the town’s 600-year history in the heart of the old town. The top floor is devoted to Albert Engström (1869–1940), an illustrator known for caricatures that mocked the failings of his time. Another room traces Eksjö’s military past. The town was long nicknamed the “town of hussars,” after these army cavalrymen. Then take a break in the courtyard, where an herb garden runs alongside the river.

To see how the upper classes lived in a small Swedish town in the 19th century, step inside Aschanska gården. The Aschan family, whose members included manufacturers and judges, lived here for three generations, from the 1830s until 1984. The entire interior of this upper-middle-class home has been preserved. Guided tours run daily in summer: book through Eksjö museum, which organizes them.

activities.text: Even in midsummer, the air turns cool at the bottom of Skurugata, a rocky gorge 800 m long and 7 m wide in places, 10 km northeast of Eksjö. In some years, snow and ice have lingered here into summer. Its origins are still debated: the most common explanation points to two parallel fractures in the rock. A 2 km loop starts at the parking lot, passes the Skuruhatt viewpoint, then descends into the gorge.

practical_info.tip: Wear sturdy shoes: in the gorge, you will need to step over boulders and fallen tree trunks.

visits.text: On July 11, 1897, explorer Salomon August Andrée, born in Gränna, took off from Svalbard with two companions in a hydrogen balloon, intending to fly over the North Pole. The balloon landed on the sea ice just over two days later, and the three men never returned. Their remains were found in 1930 on White Island (Kvitøya). Grenna Museum displays their belongings, photographs, and a replica of their ice shelter. In summer, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing 80 kronor per adult.

The layout of Brahegatan, Gränna’s main street, was no accident. Count Per Brahe the Younger founded the town in 1652 and aligned its streets toward his Brahehus Castle on the hill. Amalia Eriksson, who invented the local candy sticks, lived at number 2. Andrée’s birthplace is at number 37. Then climb Grännaberget, the hill above town: its open-air museum, dating from 1912, brings together historic buildings and offers free admission.

On a clear day, head up to Brahehus to see Lake Vättern and the island of Visingsö at your feet, 180 m below. Count Per Brahe the Younger had this castle built in the 17th century. A fire that spread from the neighboring village of Uppgränna destroyed it in 1708. The ruins, 3 km from Gränna, are accessible free of charge day and night, right beside a service area on the E4 highway.

activities.text: Swedes call it “polkagris,” literally “polka pig”: at the time, “gris” was a colloquial word for candy, and the polka was the fashionable dance. This red-and-white candy stick was invented in Gränna in 1859 by Amalia Eriksson. About a dozen candy shops in town make it before your eyes. The sugar is cooked to around 150 °C, then pulled: the air worked into it turns it white, and it is twisted by hand.

practical_info.tip: Some candy shops let you try twisting your own candy stick: it is not as easy as it looks.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry from Gränna to Visingsö (25 minutes)
to_next_leg.justification: Direct ferry crossing from Gränna to Visingsö, year-round, 25 minutes; the distance becomes 7 km, the straight-line distance between the two points, and the 25 minutes cover the crossing alone, with no waiting time.

visits.text: Prisoners of war are often blamed for setting fire to Visingsborg, but the tourist office tells a different story. On the evening of December 22, 1718, a sergeant named Johan Rasch burned some straw from his mattress in the stove to light his pipe. The fire broke out later. Only the south wing remains of the Brahe family’s castle, completed in 1662 after nearly a century of construction. The ruins are right next to the harbor: you can walk around them freely, but you cannot go inside the walls, which are at risk of collapse.

Climb the narrow, steep staircase in the bell tower of Kumlaby kyrka, a church dating from the early 12th century. In 1636, Per Brahe the Younger had the spire shortened to install a platform at the top for observing the stars. On a clear day, you can see four Swedish provinces from there. Inside, the wall paintings date from the 15th and 17th centuries. The church is open daily from mid-June to mid-August, and admission costs 20 kronor per adult.

The ruins of Näs, at the southern tip of Visingsö, are the remains of Sweden’s first royal castle. In the 12th century, the Sverker dynasty made it their residence, and four Swedish kings died on the island. The castle was destroyed in 1318. The tourist office recommends having a picnic there overlooking the lake: pick up a packed lunch at the harbor’s fish shop before you set off.

activities.text: Cycling is still the best way to see Visingsö: the island is 14 km long, and its narrow roads are mostly paved, with a few gravel stretches. Rent a bike at the harbor, then head south toward the oak forest. The Swedish navy began planting it in 1831 to provide timber for its warships. By the time the trees were large enough, ships were being built from other materials, and the forest remained.

practical_info.tip: If you don’t have a bike, take a remmalag, a horse-drawn carriage that leaves from the harbor: 40 minutes through the forest for 160 kronor per adult, daily from June to August.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry to Gränna (25 minutes), then E4 to Jönköping
to_next_leg.justification: Leg 1: ferry from Visingsö to Gränna, 7 km in 25 minutes; leg 2: E4 highway from Gränna to Jönköping, approximately 38 km in 31 minutes; driving is the main mode of transportation by both duration and distance.

activities.text: End the trip in Jönköping, 31 minutes from Gränna via the E4 highway. The station’s transportation hub, the resecentrum, brings together trains and intercity buses. Regional trains run to Nässjö, Växjö, and Gothenburg via Falköping. SJ trains also depart for Stockholm. Jönköping Airport has had no scheduled flights since 2020: to fly home, travel through another city.

practical_info.tip: The resecentrum also houses a bus station, with intercity buses to Stockholm, Gothenburg, and Malmö.

seo.h1_title: Småland in 4 Days: Crystal, Astrid Lindgren, and Lake Vättern
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Växjö with its glass museum, crosses the Kingdom of Crystal from Kosta to Målerås, then includes two nights in Vimmerby, Astrid Lindgren’s hometown. It continues through Eksjö’s wooden old town and Gränna, on the shores of Lake Vättern, before a morning of cycling on the island of Visingsö. The route ends at Jönköping train station.
seo.seo_hook: Glassblowers in Kosta, the house where Astrid Lindgren was born in Vimmerby, Eksjö’s wooden town, and Gränna’s candy sticks: Småland in 4 days.
featured_list: Kosta: Sweden’s oldest operating glassworks, open to visitors daily
Vimmerby: Astrid Lindgren’s childhood home and the Astrid Lindgrens Värld theme park
Eksjö: a wooden old town and the 800 m long Skurugata gorge
Gränna and Visingsö: the polkagris candy stick, invented in 1859, and Kumlaby’s bell tower observatory

itineraries.title: Värmland and Dalsland in 4 Days: Canal, Aqueduct, and Forests
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Karlstad to Selma Lagerlöf’s home, the lakes of Glaskogen, and the Håverud Aqueduct.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary is designed for summer: in 2026, Mårbacka, Rottneros Park, and the Dalsland Canal boats all operated from June 13 to August 22, except June 19–21, the Midsummer weekend. The boat does not depart on Sundays, so make sure your day in Håverud falls between Monday and Saturday.
itineraries.climate: Visit from mid-June to mid-August: in Karlstad, average highs reach 20 to 22 °C from June through August. Canal boats do not run on Sundays. Avoid November through March: highs stay between 0 and 5 °C, and most sites are closed or offer only a few tours.

visits.text: Ugly, perhaps, but with a fine story to tell: the woman with the broken sword on Stora torget, Karlstad’s main square, was voted “Sweden’s ugliest statue” by a television show. Fredsmonumentet, the Peace Monument, was unveiled in 1955. It commemorates the peaceful separation of Sweden and Norway in 1905. That agreement was negotiated and signed in Karlstad. Northwest of the square, also look for the statue of Sola, an 18th-century waitress nicknamed “the sun” for her cheerful disposition.

On July 2, 1865, a fire destroyed almost all of Karlstad. Only the cathedral and a few houses remained standing. Even so, Domkyrkan, the cathedral, lost its bell tower and roof that day. It had been completed in 1730 by Christian Haller, a builder from Saxony. The tower you see today was rebuilt after the fire. Then look at the layout of the surrounding streets: after the fire, the city was rebuilt on a grid, with wide, tree-lined streets.

For us, Karlstad’s most beautiful walk crosses Östra bron, the old stone bridge. At 168 m long, with twelve arches, it is Sweden’s longest stone arch bridge. Construction took fifty years, from 1761 to 1811. Legend has it that its master builder, Anders Jacobsson, took his own life for fear the bridge would collapse. That is untrue: he died at home in 1804. The bridge is about 600 m northeast of Stora torget, over the eastern branch of the Klarälven River.

If you visit just one museum in Karlstad, choose Värmlands museum, the museum of the Värmland region. It tells the region’s story from the Ice Age onward. Since 1998, a passageway has connected the oldest building, dating from 1929, to a modern wing. The museum occupies the tip of Sandgrundsudden, beside the Klarälven River. Admission costs 120 kronor and is free for visitors age 20 and under. It opens daily, staying open until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays and Fridays.

Right next to the museum, the former Sandgrund dance hall, a restaurant where people used to come to dance, now houses the Sandgrund Lars Lerin gallery. It displays watercolors by Lars Lerin, born in Munkfors in 1954. The tourist office describes him as one of the Nordic countries’ leading watercolor artists. The paintings on display change about once a year. The gallery opens Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., with admission costing 120 kronor. In summer, its terrace overlooks the river.

activities.text: At Inre hamn, the inner harbor, board a båtbuss, a water bus on the regional transit network. Karlstad is built on the delta where the Klarälven River flows into Lake Vänern. This is the largest lake in Sweden and the European Union: 5,650 km² dotted with about 22,000 islands and rocks. Route 93 takes you to the islands of Jäverön or Västra Långholmen, depending on the day. In 2026, water buses ran from June 8 to August 30, and a one-way trip cost 33 kronor.

practical_info.tip: Check the time of the last return boat in the Värmlandstrafik app before setting out. For a shorter outing, route 92 offers a narrated city tour that must be booked in advance.

visits.text: In 1909, Selma Lagerlöf became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The following year, she used the prize money to buy back Mårbacka, the estate where she was born in 1858 and which her family had lost. Between 1921 and 1923, architect Isak Gustaf Clason enlarged the small red-painted house, turning it into a manor house. In accordance with her final wishes, the house has been preserved as it was when she died in 1940. The house can only be visited on a guided tour: 220 kronor, including admission.

activities.text: Shrubs, fruit trees, vegetable beds, and flower beds: Selma Lagerlöf created the garden at Mårbacka with horticulturist Ruth Brandberg, and the current gardener is working to restore that layout. In the 19th century, her father planted a small grove here where people would drink toddy, a hot drink made with liquor, water, and sugar. Set aside some time for the estate café, which serves homemade cakes. From June through September, admission to the garden alone costs 70 kronor.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, Mårbacka was open daily from June 13 to August 23. English-language tours, offered at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. in the height of summer, must be booked in advance; other tours are mostly in Swedish.

visits.text: The loveliest detour in the Fryken Valley is Rottneros Park, a 22 ha lakeside park filled with flowers and sculptures. Selma Lagerlöf made the estate famous as Ekeby in Gösta Berling’s Saga, her first novel, published in 1891. The old manor house burned down in 1929. Starting in 1932, miller Svante Påhlson created the park, which now holds around a hundred sculptures, including works by Swedish sculptor Carl Milles. The new manor house is private.

activities.text: If you are traveling with children, leave time for the playground at Rottneros Park, named after Nils Holgersson. He is the hero of Selma Lagerlöf’s children’s book, published in 1906 and 1907: a boy who travels across Sweden on the back of a goose. The playground follows the park’s opening hours. In the height of summer, a snack stand sells light bites, with payment by card only.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the park was open from May 30 to September 6, closed on June 19, with hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., extended to 5 p.m. from June 27 to August 2. Admission: 140 kronor per adult, 50 per child. All payments are by card.

visits.text: Sundsbergs gård, an 18th-century estate near downtown Sunne, served as the model for the Björne estate in Gösta Berling’s Saga. The novel begins with a ball at Ekeby, now Rottneros, and ends here. Sunne itself appears in Selma Lagerlöf’s books as Broby. In 1893, a fire devastated the main house, and the family moved into the wing. That wing now houses the museum. The café and gallery open Wednesday through Sunday, until 4 p.m.

activities.text: Head up Tossebergsklätten, a hill north of Sunne, toward the end of the day. The narrow, steep road climbs more than 200 m in just over 2 km. At the summit, 342 m above sea level, an observation tower overlooks the Fryken Valley. You will see its long, narrow lakes. Sunne is built on the strait connecting two of them, Övre Fryken and Mellan-Fryken. The summit café opens for the season in May.

practical_info.tip: Allow time in your evening for the round trip from Sunne: the summit is about 16 km north of town as the crow flies.

visits.text: The scent of flax fills Klässbols Linneväveri, a linen weaving mill established in the village in 1920. Here you can follow the entire production process, from preparing the yarn to inspecting the finished pieces. The looms range from 19th-century handlooms to modern machines. Since 1991, the mill has supplied the linens for the Nobel banquet in Stockholm: around 500 m of tablecloth and 1,350 napkins. From May through September, the workshop and store are open daily.

activities.text: A canoe offers the best view of Glaskogen. Established in 1970, this nature reserve covers nearly 29,000 ha of forests and lakes between Arvika and Årjäng. Its name means “Gla Forest.” Its two largest lakes are Stora Gla and Övre Gla. At Lenungshammar, in the heart of the reserve, the rental center provides canoes, paddles, and life jackets. To get started, choose the easy Buvatten route, which takes 2 to 3 hours. Avoid Övre Gla in windy weather: this large lake can turn choppy in minutes.

practical_info.tip: The center does not rent canoes before May 13, in bad weather, or when the water is too cold. In midsummer, it is generally open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. To paddle or hike in the reserve, buy a Glaskogen pass at the Lenungshammar reception center; it is free for children under 16.

activities.text: Next, follow the 5 km loop trail that starts at the Lenungshammar reception center. Its first section is suitable for strollers and wheelchairs. Glaskogen has around 300 km of trails marked in orange, with wooden shelters and cabins for overnight stays. Loons, large waterbirds that dive for fish, nest near several lakes. In summer, Café Carl, right by the reception center, is a good place for a break before hitting the road.

practical_info.tip: Cell service is weak in parts of the reserve: download the map before setting out. From April 15 to September 15, fires are allowed only in designated fire pits.

visits.text: At the top of Majberget, a wooded hill in Bengtsfors, Gammelgården brings together more than 20 historic houses. This open-air museum, the largest in western Sweden, features a prosperous farmer’s homestead, a miller’s house, and a soldier’s house. A house from Nössemark, built in the 1850s, was reassembled here in 1929. The grounds are freely accessible: stroll among the houses when you arrive in the evening. In summer, guided tours sometimes provide access to the interiors for 100 kronor.

At Håverud, the Dalsland Canal had to cross a river with powerful rapids between very steep rock faces. Building conventional locks here was impossible. Engineer Nils Ericson therefore carried the canal over the river in an aqueduct: a steel-plate trough about 33 m long that spans the rapids. Boats float in this trough while the river flows beneath it. Higher still, a railroad bridge and a road bridge cross overhead. Arrive around 10 a.m. to see it before boarding the boat.

Small museum, big story: Kanalmuseet, the canal museum, has occupied the former Håverud factory office since 1971. It shows life along the Upperud River before and after the canal. Built from 1864 to 1868, the Dalsland Canal connects lakes over around 250 km. Only about 10 km had to be excavated. Its 31 locks raise boats a total of 66 m. The museum is open daily from June through August; adult admission costs 50 kronor.

Upperud Lock, close to Håverud, deserves a visit: the tourist office ranks it among the most beautiful on the canal. Its two chambers raise or lower boats by 5 m. The canal company, Dalslands Kanal AB, has its headquarters here. In summer, a former lakeside warehouse houses a small museum and a café. A ten-minute walk away, Dalslands konstmuseum, the Dalsland art museum, displays works related to nature; check its hours before visiting.

activities.text: Board at Håverud at 10:50 a.m. for the Halva Kanalrundan, the “half-canal cruise,” to Långbron. The boat passes through 10 locks, including the four consecutive locks at Håverud, which overcome an elevation difference of 9.9 m. It also crosses the aqueduct. Built in 1868, this aqueduct is held together by 33,000 rivets, none of which have needed replacing. The company operates two boats: M/S Storholmen, built in 1896, and M/S Dalslandia, which arrived on the canal in 1973. Around 2 p.m., a railcar—a small motorized train—takes you from Långbron back to Håverud.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, the boats operated from June 8 to August 22, except on Sundays and over Midsummer weekend (June 19–21). Expect to pay 510 kronor, excluding the meal. Book on the Dalslands Kanaltrafik website and pick up your tickets at the boat 30 minutes before departure. Cash is preferred: cell service is weak along the canal. Parking in Håverud is free.

visits.text: The waters of Lake Vänern lap against the gates of Köpmannebro Lock, the first lock on the Dalsland Canal. It takes boats from Lake Vänern into Lake Svanefjorden. It is also the largest lock on the canal: 35.6 m long and 7.1 m wide, the same dimensions as the locks on the Göta Canal, Sweden’s other major canal. Passing through takes only about ten minutes because the difference in water levels is very small. When the lock is operating, its café sells ice cream.

activities.text: Walk from Köpmannebro to the island of Lindön: a tunnel passes beneath the railroad tracks, then a path follows the embankment. Near Lindön Lighthouse, a rocky knoll offers a view of Lake Vänern. Plants typical of limestone soils grow on the slabs of schist along the shore. The neighboring island of Långön is also accessible on foot. Mellerud station, served by SJ trains to Gothenburg and Karlstad, is about ten minutes away by car.

practical_info.tip: Allow extra time to catch your train: Mellerud is about 11 km from Köpmannebro.

seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Karlstad, on the shores of Lake Vänern, and heads up the Fryken Valley to Mårbacka, Selma Lagerlöf’s home, and Rottneros Park. You then paddle across the lakes of Glaskogen Nature Reserve before cruising along the Dalsland Canal to the Håverud Aqueduct, where the canal crosses above a river.

itineraries.title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, visit Drottningholm Palace, the Viking town of Birka, and Gripsholm Castle, continuing on to Västerås.
itineraries.notes: Take this trip from June through August: the boat to Birka runs only from May through October; departure days vary by season. Departures from Hovgården, on the island of Adelsö, must be booked in advance with Strömma.
itineraries.climate: Visit from June through August, when average highs in Västerås range from 20 to 23 °C. Operating days for boats to Birka vary by season. August is the wettest month, so keep rain gear handy for Birka, where the visit takes place almost entirely outdoors. From November through March, highs stay below 6 °C, and the castles open only on certain days, mostly on weekends.

activities.text: Leave Stockholm heading west on Route 275 toward Vällingby, then follow the signs for Drottningholm at the Brommaplan intersection. The royal palace is only about 12 kilometers away, roughly a 15-minute drive. This itinerary includes no sightseeing in central Stockholm: the capital serves only as a starting point, with its central train station and Arlanda Airport.

practical_info.tip: At the end of the trip, Västerås is about 1 hour 10 minutes from Stockholm by car, or 55 minutes by direct train, with one departure per hour.

visits.text: The king and queen of Sweden still live at Drottningholm Palace: they have occupied the south wing since 1981. The rest of the palace is open to visitors. After the old castle burned down, Queen Hedvig Eleonora commissioned architect Nicodemus Tessin the Elder to rebuild it, beginning in 1662. UNESCO, which inscribed it on the World Heritage List in 1991, describes it as inspired by Versailles. From June through August, a 45-minute guided tour in English starts daily at 11:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m.

The Swedes call it Kina slott, the “Chinese Castle”: it is the Chinese Pavilion tucked away at the far end of Drottningholm’s park. One evening in July 1753, King Adolf Fredrik surprised Queen Lovisa Ulrika with it as a birthday gift. He had it built in secret. Several rooms retain their original silk and Chinese paper wall coverings, alongside Swedish furniture imitating the Chinese style. The pavilion opens only in summer: save it for the end of your walk through the park.

Thunder still rumbles at the Slottsteater, the Drottningholm Palace Theater, but it comes from a wooden machine. The theater, which opened in 1766, has retained its original stage machinery, still operated by hand: a wave machine, a thunder machine, and a flying chair that lifts actors into the air. This system allows rapid scenery changes with the curtain raised, in full view of the audience. After King Gustav III’s assassination in 1792, the theater was used for furniture storage before being rediscovered in 1921. The guided tour in English lasts about 1 hour and runs from May through early October (150 SEK).

activities.text: The grounds of Drottningholm Palace deserve as much time as its state rooms. In front of the facade, the Baroque garden created by the two Tessin architects, father and son, features geometric flower beds. Farther north, Gustav III began an English landscape garden, a landscaped park that imitates nature instead of trimming it into straight lines. The park is open year-round, day and night, and admission is free: enjoy it while waiting for your guided tour.

practical_info.tip: Parking at the palace costs 15 SEK per hour, for a maximum of 6 hours. For the night, look for accommodations on Ekerö, the neighboring island connected by the Tappström Bridge, on the road to Adelsö.

to_next_leg.road_type: Free ferry between Munsö and Adelsö, 6 minutes

visits.text: Three large grass-covered mounds stand in a row north of Adelsö Church: these are the Kungshögar, the “Kings’ Mounds” of Hovgården. They are part of a group of five large burial mounds, graves covered by a mound of earth. Hovgården was already a royal estate during the Viking Age, which lasted from about 800 to 1050. Together with Birka, on the neighboring island, the site has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1993. Visit it before boarding the boat, as the drive to Mariefred awaits when you return.

Only ruins remain of Alsnö hus, the brick palace that King Magnus Ladulås had built at Hovgården in the 1270s. Yet it was here that he issued the Ordinance of Alsnö in 1279. This decree exempted anyone who supplied the king with a heavily armed horseman from land tax. These exempt families formed the Swedish nobility. Nearby stands runestone U 11, carved in the 11th century with runes, the Viking alphabet. Its inscription says that a steward named Tolir had it carved for the king.

activities.text: To reach Hovgården, take the free Adelsöleden ferry, which connects the islands of Munsö and Adelsö in 6 minutes. Allow about another 10 minutes to drive to the parking lot at the hembygdsgård, the local heritage center. The dock for the boat to Birka is at least a 15-minute walk away along a gravel path through a cow pasture. This path is not recommended for people with limited mobility.

practical_info.tip: The Tappström Bridge, which leads to Ekerö, sometimes opens to let boats pass: allow an extra 15 to 20 minutes before your departure for Birka.

to_next_leg.road_type: Strömma boat, about 15 minutes, reservation required

visits.text: The guided tour, included in the boat ticket, is the best way to understand Birka, a Viking town on the island of Björkö. Founded around 750, Birka was a hub of Viking trade until it was abandoned around 975. Over 45 to 60 minutes, the guide leads you through a cemetery of burial mounds, graves beneath mounds of earth, up to the Borg, the former hillfort. The tour ends near the cross dedicated to Ansgar, the monk who founded Sweden’s first Christian community here in 831. The entire tour takes place outdoors: wear sturdy shoes.

In 2017, DNA analysis changed the story of Birka’s grave Bj 581. The warrior buried there with a sword, an ax, arrows, and two horses was a woman. Some researchers still debate this finding because the objects from the grave, excavated in the 1870s, had been moved. The grave lies near the guided tour route, beside the site of the former garrison: ask your guide to point it out.

The Birka Museum presents what excavations have revealed about the town. Of the more than 3,000 graves identified on the island, about a third have been excavated. At its peak, Birka had around 700 inhabitants, making it the size of a large village today. Allow 20 minutes to 1 hour for your visit, and pick up the free island map there before setting off on your own for Ansgar’s Chapel.

Goats and chickens roam among the houses in Birka’s reconstructed Viking quarter. You can also see Viking boats and an herb garden. Guides and staff wear Viking costumes. In July, the Vikingar på Birka festival (Vikings at Birka) brings the island to life for three weeks: this is the best time to visit with children.

activities.text: Walk 15 to 25 minutes to Ansgar’s Chapel, built in the 1930s and open throughout the season. It is named after the monk who came to preach Christianity in Birka around 830. The island also has a beach and rocks where you can swim: bring a swimsuit on hot days. Keep an eye on the time, as you have between 3 hours and 3 hours 30 minutes on the island before the return boat.

practical_info.tip: For lunch, Särimner restaurant serves a menu inspired by Viking cuisine, and Eldrimner café opens during peak season.

activities.text: The boat from Birka takes you back to the Hovgården dock on the island of Adelsö. Walk back up to the parking lot, at least 15 minutes away, then take the Adelsöleden ferry back toward Munsö. The drive to Mariefred takes you through Ekerö again: allow nearly two hours, including the ferry crossing.

practical_info.tip: The ferry is free. Its schedule is available in Trafikverket’s Trafikinfo Färjerederiet app, which also lets you call the ferry.

to_next_leg.road_type: Adelsö–Munsö ferry, then road via Ekerö
to_next_leg.justification: This is a substantial detour: you have to take the ferry from Adelsö to Munsö, cross Ekerö, then go around the southern side of Lake Mälaren to reach Mariefred; the current value includes the ferry.

visits.text: Gripsholm Castle is worth visiting as much for the story of its royal prisoners as for its rooms. King Gustav Vasa commissioned its construction in 1537 on the shores of Lake Mälaren. From 1563 to 1567, King Erik XIV imprisoned his brother Johan and Johan’s wife here. After overthrowing Erik in 1571, Johan held him here in turn before sending him to Västerås. Don’t miss Duke Charles’s chamber, one of Sweden’s best-preserved 16th-century interiors. Allow two hours for your visit.

More than 5,300 works make up Sweden’s National Portrait Collection, housed in Gripsholm Castle. King Charles XIV John, born in France as Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, founded it in the summer of 1822. It is described as the world’s oldest national portrait gallery. Each year, a portrait of a prominent Swede is added to the collection. Gustav III’s theater, installed in a tower in 1781, is among Europe’s best-preserved 18th-century theaters: save it for last.

“They traveled bravely far away to seek gold, and in the east they fed the eagle.” These words are carved on the Gripsholm runestone beside the castle’s approach. Feeding the eagle is a poetic image meaning to kill enemies. Tola had the stone erected for her son Harald, Ingvar’s brother. Harald had joined his brother’s expedition east between 1036 and 1041 and is believed to have died near the Caspian Sea. Stop here as you arrive at the castle.

Mariefred takes its name from Pax Mariae monastery, the “Peace of Mary,” run by Carthusians, monks who lived in silence. The monastery disappeared in 1526, when Gustav Vasa took possession of Gripsholm. The rådhus, or town hall, is a wooden house dating from 1784. Its Gustavian style is the Swedish form of late-18th-century Neoclassicism. The cemetery is the resting place of German writer Kurt Tucholsky, author of the 1931 novel Schloss Gripsholm (Gripsholm Castle). A self-guided walk of about 850 m connects these sites.

activities.text: Climb aboard the steam train of the Östra Södermanlands Järnväg, a museum railroad departing from Mariefred. Its rails are only 600 mm apart, much closer together than on a standard railroad: this is known as narrow gauge. The 11 km line connects Mariefred to Läggesta, a station served by regional trains, then continues to Taxinge-Näsby. Trains run most weekends from early May to late September, and often on weekdays in summer.

practical_info.tip: Trains depart near the steamboat dock. Check operating days at oslj.nu before visiting.

visits.text: Two altarpieces carved in Brussels are reason enough to stop at Strängnäs Cathedral. An altarpiece is a large decorated panel placed behind the altar. Bishop Kort Rogge gave them to the church in the late 15th century. Begun around 1250 and consecrated in 1291, the cathedral is a large brick Gothic building. It also houses the tomb of King Charles IX. In summer, it opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with a short guided tour lasting 30 minutes at 2 p.m.

Gustav Vasa was elected king of Sweden in Strängnäs in 1523. The date of his election, June 6, is now Sweden’s National Day. Roggeborgen is the castle built during Bishop Kort Rogge’s time, between 1479 and 1501. It housed Strängnäs’s secondary school from 1626 until the 1930s, then, starting in 1968, a library affiliated with the Royal Library. View it from the outside as you follow the roughly 1 km walk suggested by the tourist office.

The cobblestones of Lillgatan, Strängnäs’s oldest street, run alongside a strip of flat stones laid for pedestrians. Around it, the red houses of the old quarter survived the great fire of 1871. On the nearby hill, the Dutch-style windmill dates from 1855: it is the sixth built on this spot. Close by, Grassagården, a 17th-century burgher’s home arranged around a courtyard, houses a museum and a café. In summer, guided tours take you inside the windmill and Grassagården.

Although driven from the throne by his brother, King Erik XIV rests in a black marble sarcophagus in Västerås Cathedral. Gustav III provided this more dignified burial place in 1797. According to tradition, the cathedral was consecrated in 1271. Its tower, topped with a Baroque spire designed in 1694 by Nicodemus Tessin the Younger, rises to about 90 m. Take time to examine its 15th- and 16th-century altarpieces, including the one in St. Mary’s Chapel, carved in Antwerp around 1515.

Kyrkbacken, or “Church Hill,” extends north of Västerås Cathedral. Its cobblestone lanes, such as Skvallergränd, or “Gossip Alley,” follow a layout inherited from the Middle Ages. The small houses mostly date from the 18th and 19th centuries. Look for Mästermans källa: according to tradition, this small spring was reserved for the town’s executioner, who was forbidden to draw water from the public well. Many houses are occupied: respect private courtyards and wear sturdy shoes for the cobblestones.

If you add just one more landmark, choose Västerås Castle, built on a rise above the city. Gustav Vasa seized and rebuilt it: it took on its current appearance in the mid-16th century. The deposed King Erik XIV was held here from 1573 to 1575, after his captivity at Gripsholm. Admire it from the outside, then follow the Svartån, the river that flows through the city before emptying into Lake Mälaren.

Head north to Vallby Open-Air Museum, or Vallby friluftsmuseum, about 2 km from central Västerås. Around forty historic houses and farms from Västmanland, the region around Västerås, have been brought together here. Heritage livestock breeds live on the grounds, including Hedemora chickens and Jämtland goats. The estate’s manor house was completed in 1702. Admission to the grounds is generally free, with fees charged only for certain activities: come in summer, when the most activities are offered.

At about 9 m high and over 60 m in diameter, Anundshög is Sweden’s largest burial mound. Remains of a fire found beneath the mound date to between 210 and 540 CE, but the mound’s exact age remains disputed. Five stone ships surround it: standing stones outline the shape of a hull on the ground. The largest is over 50 m long. The site also served as a meeting place for the thing, the assembly where regional affairs were settled. In summer, guided tours are offered Monday through Friday.

“Folkvid raised all these stones for his son Heden, Anund’s brother”: this is the text on Anundshög’s large runestone. It stands in the middle of a row of 15 standing stones alongside the mound. The inscription also states that Vred carved the runes. This row appears to mark the Eriksgata, the journey each new king of Sweden made in the Middle Ages to have his election confirmed by the provincial assemblies. Walk along the row to see how the stones align.

seo.h1_title: Lake Mälaren in 3 Days: Drottningholm, Birka, and Gripsholm
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day route starts in Stockholm without lingering in the capital and follows Lake Mälaren west. You visit the royal palace of Drottningholm, take a boat from Hovgården to the Viking town of Birka, then continue to Gripsholm, Strängnäs, and Västerås. The trip ends at Anundshög, Sweden’s largest burial mound.
seo.seo_hook: Drottningholm Palace, the Viking town of Birka, Gripsholm Castle, and the cathedrals of Strängnäs and Västerås: a 3-day road trip around Lake Mälaren.
featured_list: Drottningholm: royal palace added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1991 and a theater dating to 1766 with its original stage machinery
Birka: Viking town founded around 750, with more than 3,000 graves
Hovgården: royal burial mounds and the ruins of Alsnö hus, the birthplace of the Swedish nobility in 1279
Gripsholm: Gustav Vasa’s castle, begun in 1537, and the national portrait collection
Strängnäs: cathedral consecrated in 1291 and altarpieces carved in Brussels
Västerås: Erik XIV’s tomb and Kyrkbacken’s cobblestone lanes
Anundshög: Sweden’s largest burial mound, about 9 m high

itineraries.title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, follow the Göta Canal from Söderköping to the Berg locks, then head to Vadstena and Omberg.
itineraries.notes: In 2027, the Göta Canal is open to boats from May 4 to September 30, with lock passages daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from June 15 to August 19; no boats pass from October to April. Söderköping is 16 minutes by bus from Norrköping station, and Rök is 22 km from Mjölby station.
itineraries.climate: Visit from June to August: this is the canal’s peak season, and average highs in Linköping reach 21 to 23 °C. July and August are also the rainiest months, so keep a rain jacket handy. From October to April, the canal is closed to boats, and from December to February, highs hover around 1 to 3 °C.

visits.text: Climb the 318 steps of the wooden staircase that starts at Söderköping lock and leads to the top of Ramunderberget, “Ramunder’s Mountain.” This cliff rises about 70 m above the town. From the top, the view takes in the rooftops of the old town and the Göta Canal. According to a local legend, a giant named Ramunder held a young girl named Ragnhild captive here. Benches halfway up offer a place to catch your breath. From April to September, a viewing telescope is installed in the pavilion at the summit.

Cobblestones underfoot and colorful wooden houses on either side: the Drothem neighborhood reveals Söderköping’s historic character. The town’s streets still follow their medieval layout. At its center, S:t Laurentii kyrka, St. Lawrence’s Church, was built of brick in the Gothic style in the late 13th century. Its bell tower stands separately: a 50 m wooden tower built in 1583. In summer 2026, a guided tour of the neighborhood departed from Rådhustorget square at 5:30 p.m. on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Sundays.

The Göta Canal was inaugurated at Mem, 5 km east of Söderköping, on September 26, 1832. King Charles XIV John, the former French marshal Bernadotte, attended the ceremony. Mem lock was the last lock built on the entire canal. It bridges a 3 m difference in water level between the canal and Slätbaken, a long inlet leading to the Baltic Sea. Look for the inscription from the Book of Psalms on its north wall.

activities.text: Söderköping’s best free show takes place at the lock in the canal harbor, Kanalhamnen. During peak season, from mid-June to mid-August, recreational boats pass through all day, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. A lock passage takes about 7 to 10 minutes: enough time to watch the water level change and the boat rise or fall with it. Afterward, take a seat at Smultronstället, an ice cream parlor that opened in 1982 and bills itself as Sweden’s largest ice cream restaurant. Expect to wait in line for a table; getting ice cream to go is faster.

practical_info.tip: To experience a lock passage yourself, boats depart from the harbor in summer. In 2026, a short cruise of about 3 hours traveled to Mem through two locks, from June through the end of August. The M/S Athene also offers a trip of just over 5 hours to the ruins of Stegeborg, departing at 11 a.m.

visits.text: The Carl Johans slussar lock staircase at Berg is probably the most famous on the Göta Canal. Seven adjoining locks raise boats 18.8 m from Lake Roxen to Berg harbor. The principle is simple. Each lock is a chamber closed off by watertight gates. The boat enters, the gate closes behind it, and water from the chamber above fills its chamber, raising it one step. Here, the upper gate of one chamber serves as the lower gate of the next. Allow 1 hour to follow a boat from bottom to top.

From the outside, Vreta klosters kyrka, the church of the former Vreta convent, looks like a village church. Yet it houses the tombs of four Swedish kings. One of them, Inge the Elder, founded the country’s first convent here with Queen Helena in the early 12th century. The convent later joined the Cistercian order, a religious order from France. Its ruins extend north of the church and are accessible at any time. It is a 300 m detour from the canal path. The church is open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays.

activities.text: Walk along the dragväg, the towpath once used to pull boats along the Göta Canal. Between Berg and Borensberg, it runs for about 20 km, with no cars. Along the way, a stone erected in 1932 honors the 58,000 soldiers who dug the canal. You will also pass Dubbelgångaren, “the Double,” a 9 m sculpture of rusted iron installed in 2006. Berg’s bascule bridge, built in 1998, offers an unobstructed view of Lake Roxen. The Kaffeteriet café rents bicycles in Berg and Borensberg.

practical_info.tip: In summer, the M/S Wasa Lejon leaves the Berg basin at 10 a.m. for Borensberg, a journey of about 3 hours 30 minutes through nine locks and over two canal aqueducts, bridges that carry the canal itself. It returns to Berg around 5:30 p.m. Check the season dates on the canal’s website before setting out.

visits.text: Fifteen meters of elevation change in five steps: Borenshult, northeast of central Motala, is home to the steepest lock staircase on the Göta Canal. Its five adjoining chambers connect the canal to Lake Boren, bridging a 15.3 m difference in water level. Construction took three years, and the last two locks were completed in 1825. During peak season, boats pass through one after another from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. In summer, a kiosk sells ice cream beside the locks.

Baltzar von Platen championed the Göta Canal project for nearly twenty years, but he never saw it open. This former naval officer, appointed governor-general of Norway in 1827, died in Christiania, now Oslo, on December 6, 1829. He rests in his family tomb beside the canal in Motala, at the spot he had chosen. Motala was also where the first ground was broken for the canal in May 1810.

Next, visit the Göta Canal exhibition, housed in a pavilion in the harbor district known as Dockan, between the Borenshult locks and Motala marina. It tells the story of the construction, its techniques, and its people, from Platen to Scottish engineer Thomas Telford. Across the canal lies the former site of Motala Verkstad, the workshop founded in 1822 to build machinery for the canal’s construction. The workshop later produced about 1,300 locomotives and 400 ships. The information panels are in Swedish only. Tickets are available at the nearby Mallboden café.

In our view, the castle, Vadstena slott, deserves the most time in Vadstena. This Renaissance castle, surrounded by moats (ditches filled with water), stands on the shores of Lake Vättern. King Gustav Vasa had it built as a fortress starting in 1545. His son, Duke Magnus, later transformed it into a palace. In 1552, Gustav Vasa held his wedding banquet here after marrying Katarina Stenbock. In 2026, the castle was open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. from July 6 to August 16. In summer, the wedding hall is used for opera and is closed to visitors.

Klosterkyrkan, the church of Vadstena Abbey, was built according to the instructions of Birgitta, or Bridget of Sweden, who founded her religious order here in 1346. Consecrated on February 16, 1430, it has a nave and two aisles of equal height beneath fifteen vaults. It is nicknamed the Blue Church, and its massive limestone structure does indeed have bluish hues. In the chancel, a reliquary contains remains of Birgitta and her daughter Katarina. Admission costs 30 kronor. In summer, the church is open from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays.

In the 1260s, King Valdemar had a palace built in Vadstena for political meetings and court festivities. This building, one of the oldest surviving in Sweden, houses the Sancta Birgitta Klostermuseum, the abbey museum. In 1346, King Magnus Eriksson and Queen Blanka donated it to establish the convent, which closed in 1595 during the Protestant Reformation. The museum recounts these centuries and the legacy of St. Bridget. From June to August, it is open daily; adult admission costs 110 kronor.

As you cross Rådhustorget, the town hall square and Vadstena’s oldest square, stop in front of the Rådhuset. It is Sweden’s oldest town hall. It was built in the early 15th century, shortly after Vadstena received its town charter in 1400. This charter gave the settlement the right to trade and govern itself. Between the abbey and the castle, stroll among the preserved historic houses. The town museum offers free admission and is open in the afternoons in summer.

Swedes call bobbin lace knyppling. It is made by crossing threads wound around small bobbins. Vadstena has remained a center for the finest lace. The Vadstena Lace Museum, which opened in 2005, tells its story. Around 1870, about 800 people in Vadstena and neighboring parishes earned their living from this work. When machine-made lace threatened this craft, lace-making schools were founded in 1903. In summer, the museum is open from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m., with admission costing 20 kronor.

activities.text: End the day beside Lake Vättern, Sweden’s second-largest lake after Lake Vänern. Its water is known for its clarity: many lakeside municipalities draw their drinking water from it. Walk along the waterfront near the castle. Vadstena lies on the lake’s eastern shore, so the sun sets over the water right in front of you.

practical_info.tip: Save this walk for the end of the day, when the sun sets over the lake.

visits.text: Your gaze drops 100 m into the clear waters of Lake Vättern: that is the effect of Västra väggarna, Omberg’s “western walls.” At an elevation of 172 m, this viewpoint overlooks the cliffs of the wooded hill beside the lake. On Omberg, 1,700 ha of forest form an ecopark: a large area where protecting nature takes priority over timber profits. In places, the lakeside trail runs very close to the cliff edge. Hold children by the hand, especially when the ground is wet.

Alvastra kloster, at the southern foot of Omberg, is an abbey founded in 1143 by monks from Clairvaux, France. These monks belonged to the Cistercian order, the same order as the convent at Vreta. King Sverker I had given them the land. Four kings were buried here, including Sverker I himself. The abbey fell into ruin after the Protestant Reformation. The St. Klintslingan also starts at Alvastra: a 5 km loop with two steep climbs.

activities.text: Lace up your shoes at the Stocklycke parking lot, the ecopark’s visitor hub, to follow Ellen Keys led, a 6.1 km trail. It is named after the writer Ellen Key, who had her house, Strand, built at the foot of Omberg in 1910. The trail passes through beech forests: on Omberg, beech reaches its northern limit in eastern Scandinavia. A steep climb leads to Hjässan, the highest point, at just over 260 m. From there, the view stretches across Lake Vättern, Lake Tåkern, and the plain. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes.

practical_info.tip: Short version: starting at Stocklycke, the beech trail is 650 m long and suitable for wheelchairs and strollers. Lake Tåkern, visible from the summit, has its nature visitor center at Glänås; in 2026, it was open Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., May 1 through August 16, with free admission.

visits.text: If you could see only one runestone in Sweden, choose Rökstenen, the Rök Stone, beside the village church. Runes are the alphabet of the ancient Scandinavians. Standing 2.4 m tall, the stone was probably carved in the early 9th century. Its roughly 760 characters form the longest known runic inscription from before Christianity. A father, Varin, honors his deceased son, Vämod, with partly coded riddles. It was found in the 19th century, embedded in the church wall. A roof has protected it since 2020. Allow 30 minutes here.

seo.h1_title: Göta Canal in 3 Days: Berg Locks, Vadstena, and Omberg
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary follows the Göta Canal from Söderköping to the Berg and Borenshult locks, then runs along Lake Vättern to Vadstena and Omberg. Watch boats navigate the lock staircases, visit Saint Bridget’s Abbey and Vadstena Castle, then walk high above the lake before visiting the Rök runestone.
seo.seo_hook: Berg Locks, Platen’s tomb in Motala, Vadstena’s abbey and castle, and Omberg’s cliffs: the Göta Canal in 3 days, from Söderköping to Rök.

itineraries.title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Lund to the castles and orchards of Österlen, then on to Helsingborg and the cliffs of Kullaberg.
itineraries.notes: Visit from May to September: Glimmingehus is open daily, Sofiero and Kärnan keep summer hours, and Kivik’s burial chamber is open to visitors. In winter, Kärnan and the Kullaberg naturum visitor center close, and Glimmingehus opens only for a few events.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to September, with average highs in Helsingborg of 16 °C in May and 21 °C in July and August. Avoid November to March: short days, temperatures of 2 to 7 °C, frequent rain, and winter hours at most attractions. Keep a windbreaker handy for the cliffs of Kullaberg and the summit of Stenshuvud, which are exposed to sea winds.

visits.text: The finest introduction is Lunds domkyrka, Lund Cathedral. It is Romanesque in style, with rounded arches and thick walls. Its high altar was consecrated in 1145, when Lund was already the seat of an archbishop. The city was Danish at the time, as Skåne did not become Swedish until 1658. Look up at the apse, the rounded section behind the altar: its mosaic dates from 1927. The church opens daily, starting at 8 a.m. on weekdays and 9:30 a.m. on weekends.

“Finn, Finn, lay the last stone!” This cry is at the heart of the legend of Lund Cathedral’s crypt. According to the tale, the giant Finn was building the church in exchange for the monk Lars’s eyes, unless Lars could guess his name. Once his identity was revealed, Finn tried to topple the pillars in anger, but daylight turned him to stone. His statue still clings to a column. The crypt dates from 1123, and each of its 27 pillars is different. Come before noon, ahead of the crowds arriving to see the astronomical clock.

Lundagård, the large park stretching out below the cathedral, is the historic heart of Lund University, founded in 1666. At the edge of the park stands Universitetshuset, the main building, inaugurated in 1882 by King Oscar II. Look at its roof: four sphinxes stand guard there. The originals, carved from poor-quality stone, were removed in less than thirty years and replaced in the 1990s. Walk across the park: the historical museum is in the same garden.

Four enormous carved stones stand at the entrance to Historiska museet, Lund University’s historical museum. They form the Hunnestad Monument, erected around the year 1000 on Skåne’s southern coast. They include runestones, covered in inscriptions in the old Scandinavian alphabet, and stones carved with images. Lund’s tourist office describes this museum as Sweden’s second-largest archaeology museum. Check the hours: it is open only Wednesday through Sunday, from noon to 4 p.m.

Brick, stone, and half-timbering: at Kulturen, Lund’s open-air museum, moving from house to house takes you from one era to another. Opened in 1892, it brings together more than 30 historic buildings across two downtown blocks. The oldest, Dekanhuset (the dean’s house), dates from the Middle Ages. Admission costs 150 kronor per adult and is free for visitors ages 18 and under. From May to August, the museum opens daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., until 8 p.m. on Thursdays; the rest of the year, it is closed on Mondays.

Drafts are on display here, and that is the appeal of Skissernas museum, Lund’s museum of sketches. Since 1934, it has collected more than 30,000 designs for public artworks intended for squares and buildings: sculpture models and drawings for murals or reliefs. You can see how Henri Matisse, Diego Rivera, and Henry Moore prepared their commissions. The museum is closed on Mondays. Admission costs 100 kronor, but is free for visitors ages 25 and under and on Thursdays from 5 to 7 p.m.

activities.text: End the day in the peaceful surroundings of Botaniska trädgården, Lund University’s botanical garden. Established in 1690, it has occupied its current site since 1862. You can wander freely among tall trees and flower beds across its 8 hectares, roughly the size of ten soccer fields. Admission is free, and the garden opens daily from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m., so you can visit after the museums close.

practical_info.tip: The garden’s greenhouses are being renovated, with reopening announced for 2027: only the outdoor garden is open to visitors.

activities.text: If you are in the cathedral at noon, stay for the Horologium mirabile Lundense, “the marvelous clock of Lund,” built around 1425. At the top, two knights cross swords whenever the hour strikes. Then the Three Wise Men and their servants parade before the Virgin Mary. A small hidden organ plays the medieval hymn In dulci jubilo. The calendar on the dial ends in 2123, when a new one will need to be installed. The clock comes to life at noon and 3 p.m., and on Sundays at 1 p.m. and 3 p.m.

practical_info.tip: Monday through Saturday, a short introductory talk takes place at 11:45 a.m.: arrive early for a good spot facing the clock.

activities.text: Have lunch at Saluhallen, the covered market on Mårtenstorget square in central Lund. Since 1909, this market has served as a gathering place for locals. It is a convenient stop for a quick meal between visits. On the same square, Lunds konsthall, an art exhibition hall opened in 1957, is worth a look if you have ten minutes.

practical_info.tip: In good weather, take your meal to go and picnic on the lawns of Lundagård.

visits.text: A water-filled moat, a drawbridge, and bare stone walls: Glimmingehus looks like a storybook fortress set amid the fields. The Danish knight Jens Holgersen Ulfstand had it built between 1499 and 1506. Its architect, the German stonemason Adam van Düren, had also worked on Lund Cathedral. The Swedish National Heritage Board describes it as the best-preserved medieval castle in the Nordic countries. Admission costs 100 kronor and is free for visitors ages 18 and under.

activities.text: Take the guided tour of Glimmingehus, included in your ticket, to spot the castle’s traps. False doors and dead-end corridors awaited attackers. Through holes above the passageways, defenders poured boiling pitch, a heated resin, onto anyone forcing their way in. The walls are 2.4 m thick at the base. From July 1 to August 9, an English-language tour departs daily at 12:30 p.m.

practical_info.tip: The castle opens daily from May to September, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., with hours extended to 6 p.m. from July 1 to August 9. In April and October, it opens only on weekends and during Swedish school breaks.

visits.text: Established in 1986, Stenshuvud National Park covers just 374 hectares, including the sea, or less than 4 km². Yet it encompasses deciduous forests, meadows, sandy heathland, and marshes. The naturum visitor center, dedicated to the park’s natural environment, is at the main entrance, signposted from Route 9. The park is home to the hazel dormouse, a small nocturnal rodent, and the European tree frog, a tiny frog that climbs trees. Stop at the naturum visitor center before your walk to get your bearings on the trails.

activities.text: If you take just one hike, choose Stenshuvud’s red trail: 2 km round-trip, about 1 hour. It passes through woods of hornbeams and old oaks, then climbs the hill. The hill has three summits; the northern one is the highest, at 97 m above sea level. From there, the view stretches across Hanö Bay. Remains of an Iron Age rampart survive near the summit. Wear sturdy shoes: the climb alternates between steps and rocky stretches.

practical_info.tip: The park is open year-round. Park only in designated parking lots.

activities.text: Stenshuvud’s blue trail is a short 1 km loop, taking about 30 minutes, between the naturum visitor center and the sea. Along the waterfront, you pass Krivareboden, a former eel fishermen’s hut. This is the park’s easiest trail, adapted for people with limited mobility. Save it for the end of the day, when the climb up the hill has tired you out.

practical_info.tip: With children, this trail is enough: it avoids the steps on the hill.

activities.text: After the climb, nothing beats an hour on Stenshuvud’s sandy beach at the foot of the hill. Swimmers flock here in summer. The yellow trail, a 4 km loop taking about 1 hour 30 minutes, also leads to the beach. It passes through the arboretum at the north entrance, planted in the late 19th century, then returns through the oak forest and along the beach. Avoid sandals: this trail is very rocky in places.

practical_info.tip: The yellow trail starts at the main entrance: bring water for the loop.

visits.text: In 1748, two farmers quarrying stone near Kivik stumbled upon a stone cist made of engraved slabs. They had just discovered Kiviksgraven, also called Kungagraven, “the king’s tomb.” This Bronze Age cairn, an enormous mound of stones raised over a tomb around 1400 BCE, measures 75 m in diameter. Inside, eight original slabs depict ships, a chariot drawn by two horses, and musicians playing the lur, a long bronze horn. The burial chamber is open to visitors only during the warmer months: check opening hours at bredaror.se.

Apple orchards line the roads: you are in the heartland of Kiviks Musteri, Kivik’s juice and cider company. Its information center, Äpplets hus (the house of the apple), opened in 1996 and tells the story of fruit growing in the village since 1888. Around 70 apple varieties grow in the orchards around Kivik. Admission is free. At the shop, sample the juices and ciders before buying.

activities.text: You will spend the evening at Kivik’s harbor, a small fishing port facing Hanö Bay. The village, with fewer than a thousand residents, is known for its apples but also for its herring. Look for it on the menus of the harbor restaurants. Every July, Kiviks marknad, a large three-day fair, takes over the streets. If your trip falls during the fair, book your overnight stay well in advance.

practical_info.tip: The fair generally runs from the third Monday in July through the following Wednesday.

visits.text: Helsingborg’s best viewpoint is 35 m up, at the top of Kärnan, the brick keep overlooking the city. It was built in the 1310s for the king of Denmark. It is the only surviving part of a large Danish fortress, demolished on the orders of the king of Sweden starting in the 1680s. Its walls are 4.5 m thick at the base. From the top, you can see Helsingør, Denmark, 4 km away across the Øresund.

Rådhuset, Helsingborg’s city hall, is recognizable by its tall clock tower and richly decorated red brick facades. Inaugurated in 1897, it was designed by Alfred Hellerström, who combined Italian, Dutch, and German influences. The same architect had restored Kärnan a few years earlier. Inside, ten stained-glass windows based on designs by painter Gustaf Cederström tell the city’s history. Allow twenty minutes to walk around the building and view its facades.

A great astronomer left his mark on Sankta Maria kyrka, St. Mary’s Church in Helsingborg. Tycho Brahe, the 16th-century Danish scholar, had an epitaph, or funerary plaque, installed here for his daughter Kristina, who died of the plague in 1576. This red brick Gothic church was completed around 1450. Its altarpiece, a large carved panel behind the altar, comes from Germany. Its pulpit, the raised platform from which sermons are delivered, was carved in 1615. For a guided tour, contact the parish in advance.

If it rains, take shelter at Dunkers kulturhus, Helsingborg’s cultural center, which opened in 2002. Designed by Danish architect Kim Utzon, it houses the city museum, which traces Helsingborg’s history from the Ice Age to the present day. The building also hosts art exhibitions. It is named after industrialist Henry Dunker (1870–1962), whose foundation funded it. Check the program online: temporary exhibitions change regularly.

In late spring, thousands of rhododendrons bloom at Sofiero above the Øresund, the strait separating Sweden from Denmark. According to the Skåne tourist office, the park has more than 10,000 rhododendrons representing nearly 500 varieties. King Gustaf VI Adolf, a keen gardener, started this collection after receiving the estate as a wedding gift in 1905. From mid-May through late August, admission costs 155 kronor (145 online), is free for visitors age 17 and under, and can be paid by card only.

Sofiero Castle, built in the Dutch Renaissance style, was constructed in 1865 for Prince Oscar, the future King Oscar II, and his wife Sophie. Gustaf VI Adolf used it as his summer residence until 1973, then bequeathed it to the city of Helsingborg. Each season, the castle hosts an exhibition. Admission is included with the park ticket. The estate is open from late March through fall, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. through late August, then until 5 p.m. on weekdays.

Standing 78.5 m above the sea, Kullens fyr, the lighthouse in Kullaberg Nature Reserve, is described by the reserve as the brightest in Scandinavia. Its optical system, delivered in 1900, has three large Fresnel lenses, stepped lenses that concentrate light. They rotate four times per minute, and each rotation produces three flashes, visible from about 50 km away. Right next door, the naturum Kullaberg visitor center has a saltwater aquarium. The naturum visitor center was open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. in July and August 2025.

Mölle looks like a peaceful fishing port, yet this village caused a stir in the late 19th century. Men and women swam together here, a practice considered daring at the time. This mixed bathing drew visitors from across Sweden and Europe. Until World War I, a weekly train even came from Berlin. Today, the harbor holds around 130 boats. Come at sunset, facing the Kattegat, the stretch of sea between Sweden and Denmark.

activities.text: You will follow Vandringsstigen på Västra Kullaberg, the discovery trail through the western part of Kullaberg Nature Reserve. This roughly 5 km loop starts at the naturum visitor center near the lighthouse. It passes Lahibia Cave, Ransvik Cove, the cliffs of Josefinelust, and Visit Cave at the foot of the north face. The reserve has around twenty caves. The main trail is fairly easy, but some detours down to the sea are steep: hiking shoes are essential, and take care near the cliff edges.

practical_info.tip: The trail guide, in Swedish, can be downloaded from kullabergsnatur.se. Parking is free in designated lots, 500 m from the lighthouse. Dogs must stay on a leash.

visits.text: Helsingborg’s most enjoyable museum may well be outdoors: Fredriksdal, which opened in 1923 around an 18th-century manor house. In the 1960s, houses and shops from the city center were dismantled and rebuilt here, brick by brick. Herb, rose, and wildflower gardens surround the buildings, as does an open-air theater in the French Baroque style. The park remains accessible year-round, while opening seasons vary for the buildings. Tickets start at 120 kronor.

activities.text: You’ll return the car in Helsingborg before heading to Knutpunkten, “the crossroads,” the city’s main station, which brings together trains, buses, and ferries. Ferries to Helsingør, Denmark, cross the Øresund in about 20 minutes, with more than 70 departures a day. Regional Øresundståg trains also connect Helsingborg with Copenhagen. Around 50,000 travelers pass through Knutpunkten each day: arrive early during rush hour.

practical_info.tip: The drive from Kullaberg is included in the previous leg: this stop only covers the visit to Fredriksdal and departure.

seo.h1_title: Skåne in 4 Days: Lund, Helsingborg, Kullaberg, and Österlen
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip explores Scania (Skåne in Swedish), at the southern tip of Sweden. It starts in Lund with its Romanesque cathedral, then crosses Österlen, taking in the fortress of Glimmingehus, Stenshuvud hill, and Kivik’s orchards. It ends in Helsingborg, with Sofiero Park and Kullaberg lighthouse.
seo.seo_hook: Lund Cathedral, Glimmingehus Castle, Kivik’s apple trees, and Kullaberg’s cliffs: a 4-day road trip through Skåne in southern Sweden.
featured_list: Lund: an astronomical clock from 1425 that comes to life at noon
Glimmingehus: a medieval fortress preserved intact amid the fields
Stenshuvud: a summit 97 m above Hanö Bay
Kivik: the King’s Grave, a Bronze Age burial mound 75 m in diameter
Helsingborg: the Kärnan keep, 4 km from Denmark
Kullaberg: Scandinavia’s most powerful lighthouse and around twenty caves
