itineraries.title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen
itineraries.subtitle: Explore City Hall, Gamla Stan, Södermalm, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen over 2 days on foot, by ferry, and by tram.
itineraries.notes: The City Hall tower is closed for renovation and is not expected to reopen until 2029: only the halls can be visited, with a guide. From late September to early January, Skansen closes at 3 p.m. on weekdays and 4 p.m. on weekends, and the Royal Palace closes at 4 p.m.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with highs of 16 to 24 °C and up to 18 hours of daylight in June. From November through February, highs stay between 1 and 5 °C, with only 6 to 9 hours of daylight: dress warmly for walking. June, July, and August are also the rainiest months, so keep a raincoat handy.

visits.text: It is best to book ahead for Stockholm City Hall, the Stadshuset: entry is only possible on a guided tour at a set time. The tour lasts 45 minutes and is offered in English or Swedish. It takes you through the Blue Hall, where the Nobel Prize banquet is held. Its brick walls are not blue, however: the architect abandoned the planned blue tiles during construction. Next comes the Golden Hall, covered in more than 18 million small mosaic tiles. Tickets go on sale online one week in advance, and the ticket office opens at 8:30 a.m.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre stockholms stadshus et stockholms slott, environ 1250 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 6 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 15 min de marche.

visits.text: On May 7, 1697, a fire almost completely destroyed the fortified castle of Tre Kronor, the “Three Crowns.” In its place, architect Nicodemus Tessin designed the current Baroque palace, Stockholms slott. It has more than 600 rooms. It is still the king’s official residence and workplace. The ticket includes admission to the Royal Apartments and the Tre Kronor Museum, devoted to the lost castle. It also includes the Treasury, where the royal regalia—crowns, scepters, and other symbols of kingship—are displayed. Expect to pay 220 Swedish kronor, or 240 from May through September.

activities.text: If you arrive at the palace around noon, stay in the outer courtyard of Stockholms slott for the changing of the guard. Soldiers of the Royal Guards replace the previous contingent after a parade that brings them to the palace. The ceremony lasts about 40 minutes. It starts at 12:15 p.m. Monday through Saturday and at 1:15 p.m. on Sundays and public holidays. Times may change: check them the day before on the website of the Swedish Armed Forces, which provide the guard.

practical_info.tip: Changing of the guard: 12:15 p.m. Monday through Saturday, 1:15 p.m. on Sundays and public holidays, in the outer courtyard. The palace is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. October through April, and until 5 p.m. May through September.

to_next_leg.justification: Walk between two nearby stops downtown; the routing engine calculated a driving route due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance, while the indicated walk of 0.2 km in 3 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Storkyrkan means “the great church”: it is Stockholm’s oldest church. Near the choir, the statue of Saint George Slaying the Dragon was unveiled in 1489. Sten Sture the Elder, who ruled Sweden at the time, commissioned it after his 1471 victory over the king of Denmark. Also look for Vädersolstavlan, the “Sun Dog Painting,” the oldest color image of Stockholm. It depicts a halo seen on April 20, 1535: ice crystals in the clouds caused false suns to shine around the real one. Admission is 120 kronor, including an audio guide.

to_next_leg.justification: Walk between two nearby stops downtown; the routing engine calculated a driving route due to one-way streets, a detour, or a zero distance, while the indicated walk of 0.1 km in 2 minutes is correct.

activities.text: Take time to get lost in Gamla Stan, the old town founded in the 13th century on the island of Stadsholmen. At its center, Stortorget square was the site of the “Stockholm Bloodbath.” In November 1520, King Christian II of Denmark had 90 people executed there over three days, mostly Swedish nobles. On the square, the former Stock Exchange houses the Nobel Prize Museum. Then walk down the 36 steps of Mårten Trotzigs gränd, Stockholm’s narrowest alley: just 90 cm at its narrowest point. It starts on Prästgatan.

practical_info.tip: Mårten Trotzigs gränd is accessible from 6 a.m. to midnight. It connects Prästgatan to Västerlånggatan.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre gamla stan et monteliusvagen, environ 1000 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 6 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 12 min de marche.

activities.text: If the sky clears toward the end of the day, head up to Monteliusvägen, a 416-meter path clinging to the northern cliffs of Södermalm. Södermalm is the large island south of the old town. The path is named after archaeologist Oscar Montelius. The view stretches across the water to City Hall, Riddarholmen Church, and Lake Mälaren. Sunset is photographers’ favorite time here. From December through March, snow is not cleared from the path: wear shoes with good traction.

practical_info.tip: Nearest subway stations: Slussen or Mariatorget. The path can be slippery in winter, despite the railing.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre monteliusvagen et fotografiska, environ 1800 m de marche réelle comptés 2 km : l'ancienne durée de 6 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 23 min de marche.

visits.text: The building is old; the images are new. Fotografiska, a photography museum that opened in 2010, occupies a former brick customs house built in 1906 in the Art Nouveau style. Its temporary exhibitions change throughout the year. Then head to the top floor: according to the tourist office, its café offers one of Stockholm’s finest panoramic views. The museum is open every day until 11 p.m., so save it for the evening.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry 82 from Slussen to Allmänna gränd, then a 400 m walk

visits.text: In 1891, educator Artur Hazelius opened Skansen on a hill on the island of Djurgården. According to Skansen, it is the world’s oldest open-air museum: a village of historic houses brought here from across Sweden. Hazelius bought about 150 of them throughout the country to reassemble here. In the farms and houses open to visitors, hosts explain what life was like in each period. The bakery recreates an 1870s shop and sells cinnamon buns. Tickets are cheaper online. Only card payments are accepted on site.

activities.text: Next, head to the zoo area, as Skansen also showcases Scandinavia’s wild animals. Brown bears, moose, reindeer, lynx, otters, and gray seals live here. The grounds cover 30 hectares, the equivalent of about 40 soccer fields, so good walking shoes are essential. Short talks lasting 15 minutes introduce the horses and seals at times listed in Skansen’s calendar. If you’re visiting with children, add Lill-Skansen, the small children’s zoo, which is included in your ticket.

practical_info.tip: From late September to early January, Skansen is open from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekends. In summer, expect hours of 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre skansen et vasamuseet, environ 950 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 5 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 12 min de marche.

visits.text: Entering the Vasamuseet is a jaw-dropping experience: a 69-meter warship towers beneath the roof. The Vasa sank on August 10, 1628, after sailing 1,300 meters: too much weight high up made it unstable. It was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom. The shipworm, a mollusk that devours wood, does not live in the Baltic’s low-salinity water. This partly explains why more than 98% of the ship is original. A 25-minute guided tour is included in the ticket.

Kungsträdgården means “the king’s garden,” but in 1430, records gave it the more modest name “the king’s vegetable garden.” In May 1971, the park witnessed the “Battle of the Elms.” Plans called for cutting down old elm trees to build a subway entrance, and residents chained themselves to the trees. The elms were saved, and the subway entrances were placed on either side of the park. In spring, 63 Japanese cherry trees planted in 1998 bloom and draw crowds. In winter, an ice rink is set up.

activities.text: Finish underground in Stockholm’s subway, often nicknamed “the world’s longest art gallery”: more than 90 of its 100 stations are decorated. Kungsträdgården station, 34 meters below ground, echoes the colors of the park’s former Baroque garden: red gravel, white marble, and green planting beds. Then take the Blue Line. At T-Centralen, blue vines surround silhouettes of the workers who built the station. Continue to Solna Centrum, where a painted forest stretches along the walls. A regular SL ticket is all you need.

practical_info.tip: A regular SL ticket is all you need: the art can be viewed from the platforms. The Blue Line starts at its terminus, Kungsträdgården, and Solna Centrum is on Line 11.

seo.h1_title: Stockholm in 2 Days: Gamla Stan, the Vasa Museum, and Skansen
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Stockholm is car-free, with travel on foot, by ferry, tram, and subway. The first day takes you from City Hall to the Royal Palace and the narrow streets of Gamla Stan, then over to Södermalm, from the Monteliusvägen path to Fotografiska. The second day is devoted to the island of Djurgården, with Skansen and the Vasa Museum, before ending your stay in the subway’s art-filled stations.
seo.seo_hook: Stockholm in 2 days without a car: City Hall, the Royal Palace, Gamla Stan, views from Monteliusvägen, the Vasa Museum, Skansen, and subway art.

itineraries.title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, follow Sweden’s High Coast from the Högakustenbron bridge to the island of Ulvön, via Skuleberget and Högbonden.
itineraries.notes: Go from late June to mid-August: in 2026, the Högbonden boat ran daily from June 22 to August 16, with departures on some weekends outside this period as well. It cannot dock in strong winds. The Ulvön ferry departs from Köpmanholmen year-round, and the train stations in Härnösand and Örnsköldsvik sit at either end of the route.
itineraries.climate: Go from mid-June to mid-August: in Härnösand, average highs reach 18 °C in June, 21 °C in July, and 20 °C in August. August is also the wettest month, so keep a rain jacket handy. From November to March, highs stay between -2 and 3 °C, and the Högbonden boat does not run.

visits.text: There is no better gateway to the High Coast than Högakustenbron, the High Coast Bridge. Opened in 1997, it spans the mouth of the Ångermanälven River for 1,867 m. Its two towers rise about 180 m above the water. Between them, the roadway stretches 1,210 m without any supports beneath it, suspended from large cables. Stop at the Hornöberget rest area at the north end of the bridge for a view taking in both the bridge and the river. If traveling by train, get off at Härnösand station, about 25 km to the south.

Nordingrå Church took seven years to build and was completed in 1825 on the shore of Vågsfjärden Bay. If the door is open, look at the altarpiece, the carved panel behind the altar: it was made in Brussels. To the east are the ruins of the medieval church, whose oldest sections date from the early 13th century. Around it, twelve small church stables remain out of the roughly 80 that once stood here. Worshippers sheltered their horses in them during services, as many traveled from far away. Park near the church and explore on foot.

Mannaminne, in Häggvik, is an open-air museum, but it is far from a neatly arranged historic village: everything mingles here. Started in 1980 by artist Anders Åberg and his wife Barbro, it has more than 50 buildings on a wooded hill. You will find a Norwegian-style wooden church built in 2000, streetcars from several countries, a Stockholm subway car, and a Swedish Saab 35 Draken fighter jet. In 2026, the site was open daily from May 30 to August 31, with admission costing 180 kronor and free entry for visitors under 18. Allow at least 2 hours 30 minutes.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Häggvik and Fällsvik, then a forest road

visits.text: You can leave your car in Barsta, a former fishing village just east of Rotsidan Nature Reserve. On the hill near the old harbor stands Barsta Chapel, built around 1650 and almost unchanged since 1699. The parish describes it as the best-preserved fishermen’s chapel in its diocese. From there, the Världsarvsleden, a 100 km hiking trail that crosses the reserve, leads to the rock slabs.

activities.text: Beneath your feet, the rock is smooth and almost flat, like an enormous slab laid beside the sea. Rotsidan Nature Reserve protects about 4 km of coastline made up of slabs of diabase, a dark rock polished by the waves. Dwarf pines and spruces grow along the edges. In the cracks grows strandtrav, a small plant found nowhere else in Sweden but this coast. During storms from the southeast, the slabs send waves surging high up the shore: stay well back from the edge.

practical_info.tip: From the parking lot, a gravel path with wooden ramps reaches the sea in 600 m; it is suitable for strollers and wheelchairs. On the slabs, designated fire pits and a supply of firewood let you grill your meal.

visits.text: Bönhamn is the High Coast’s best-loved old fishing village. Its tightly clustered boathouses surround a small, naturally sheltered harbor. Fishing was long the main source of income here. Today, this is where the boat to the island of Högbonden departs. Stroll along the docks toward the end of the day, once the day visitors have left. A harbor café also serves lunch, and there is a fee for parking in the village.

Next, stop by Bönhamn Chapel, a small fishermen’s chapel. It was not built here. In the 16th century, fishermen from Gävle, a coastal town farther south, leased these fishing waters. They built the chapel on the islet of Höglosmen, north of Högbonden. In the early 19th century, it was dismantled and reassembled in Bönhamn, on the mainland. In winter, it was also used to store fishing equipment. Admission is free, and concerts are held here in summer.

If the sea is calm, the M/S Ronja boat takes you to Högbonden, a steep island off Bönhamn, in 15 minutes. Its lighthouse, first lit in 1909, is the second-highest in Sweden by elevation: its light shines 75 m above the sea. Three keepers worked here when it opened. At its peak, 21 people lived on the island, and a classroom occupied the attic. The keepers’ houses now accommodate a hostel. In 2026, it was open on weekends from May 29 to June 21, daily from June 22 to August 16, and then on weekends again from August 17 to September 27. The café was open daily from June 22 to August 16.

activities.text: Walk around Högbonden along the nature reserve’s trails. The terrain is hilly and covered with stones. The island’s rock splits easily, and the sea has carved caves into it. The largest, Bondstugan, opens onto the shore just south of the lighthouse. The soil is thin everywhere: the island has been gradually rising out of the sea since the end of the Ice Age, and waves have washed away the soil as it emerged. Wear sturdy shoes and allow plenty of time before the last boat.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, M/S Ronja operated four departures a day from June 22 to August 16, from Bönhamn or Barsta. It cannot dock in strong winds: check the current year’s schedule and book before you go.

to_next_leg.road_type: Boat to Bönhamn harbor, then drive to the E4 heading north
to_next_leg.justification: Two segments: a short boat crossing from Högbonden to Bönhamn harbor, then about 40 km by road to the E4 and Skuleberget; driving is the main mode of transportation because the fixed 2 hours of waiting time does not match this short crossing.

visits.text: About 10,500 years ago, the summit of Skuleberget was just a 9 m rock sticking out of the sea. Naturum Höga Kusten, the visitor center at the foot of the mountain, explains why. During the Ice Age, a layer of ice about 3 km thick pressed down on the region. When it melted, the land, freed of that weight, began to rise. It is still rising by about 8 mm a year. According to UNESCO, no other known place has risen as much: this is why the High Coast was listed in 2000. Admission is free.

activities.text: Climb to the summit of Skuleberget via Grottstigen, the “cave trail”: a very steep 600 m climb requiring 30 to 40 minutes of effort. A detour leads to Kungsgrottan, the King’s Cave, carved out by ice, water, and waves. It owes its name to a visit by King Charles XI in the 17th century. At the top, the 900 m Kalottstigen loop follows the ancient shoreline. It now lies 286 m above sea level: the highest ancient shoreline in the world. Head back down via the less steep Södra Bergsstigen in about 1 hour.

practical_info.tip: Avoid Grottstigen in wet weather, with young children, or with a dog: take Södra Bergsstigen instead (2.5 km, 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes). Dogs must remain on a leash in the nature reserve.

activities.text: Swedes say vajerledsklättring, “climbing along a cable”: it is their word for via ferrata. On Skuleberget’s roughly 250 m-high east face, four climbing routes are equipped with a steel cable that you remain attached to throughout. The easiest, the white route, is the first via ferrata in Sweden and the Nordic countries: brothers Arne and Gunnar Nordin began equipping it in June 1987. Helmets and harnesses are provided on-site, with no reservation required.

practical_info.tip: Open from May through October on days when the rock is dry; you must weigh at least 40 kg, and each adult may accompany only one child. If heights scare you, take the chairlift on the western slope instead: the ride up takes about 20 minutes, and the summit cabin serves coffee and simple meals in summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road to Köpmanholmen, then the M/F Ulvön ferry to Ulvöhamn
to_next_leg.justification: Two segments: about 25 km by road from Skuleberget to Köpmanholmen, then the crossing on the M/F Ulvön ferry (about 20 km); the 110 minutes cover travel time only, waiting time is added by the program, and ferry schedules need to be rechecked.

visits.text: Ulvö gamla kapell, the old chapel on Ulvön, dates to 1622. At the time, fishermen from Gävle, a coastal town farther south, spent every summer on the island fishing for herring. In 1719, painter Roland Johansson Öberg covered the interior with scenes from the Bible in a simple folk style. In 1888, demolition of the chapel had been authorized. Two years later, King Oscar II donated 200 riksdaler, the currency of the time, during a visit to help save it. In summer, free guided visits are available from noon to 3 p.m.

Small, but the best first stop on the island: the Ulvön museum recreates a 20th-century fisherman’s home. You can see his boathouse and gistvall, the meadow where nets were spread out to dry. Screens tell the story of fishing and the salting houses, workshops where fish were salted. Ulvön is where the tradition of surströmming began in the 16th century: fermented Baltic herring with a very strong smell. Admission is free.

activities.text: Climb Lotsberget, the hill overlooking Ulvöhamn, the harbor village. The trail climbs almost continuously, largely via a staircase. At the top, the view stretches across Ulvöhamn’s wooden houses and the islands of the archipelago. The village lines the Ulvösund strait, which separates Norra Ulvön, the northern island, from Södra Ulvön, the southern island. Go up in the late afternoon, after the excursion boats have left: you will have the view almost to yourself.

practical_info.tip: Explore Ulvöhamn on foot along its main street, Hamngatan, where the ferries dock. Allow about 45 minutes for the climb up and back down.

activities.text: If you have half a day to spare, rent a bike and head to Sandviken at the northern tip of Ulvön. This fishing hamlet, protected since 2005, is considered the best preserved in Ångermanland, the province along this coast. Around twenty gray cabins, rebuilt after a fire in 1786, line a bay with white sand. The sjöbodar, waterfront cabins, were used to store fish and nets. Families lived in the kokhus, the house where the cooking was done. A chapel dating to 1867, with a separate bell tower, overlooks the bay.

practical_info.tip: Bikes can be rented at the Ulvön kiosk or the ice cream shop by the harbor. The island has no buses and almost no cars. Some houses in Sandviken are available to rent in summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: M/F Ulvön ferry to Köpmanholmen, then 24 km by road to Örnsköldsvik
to_next_leg.justification: Two segments: the crossing on the M/F Ulvön ferry to Köpmanholmen (about 22 km), then 24 km by road to Örnsköldsvik; the 110 minutes cover travel time only, waiting time is added by the program, and ferry schedules need to be rechecked.

visits.text: The city’s rooftops, harbor, and jagged coastline spread out before you: from the Varvsberget viewpoint, you can take in Örnsköldsvik at a glance. This hill overlooks downtown. It is also home to Paradiskullen, the city’s ski jump, visible from the streets below. In summer, Paradisliften, a lift that reopened in 2022, runs from downtown to the summit. The viewpoint is also easy to reach by car. It makes a good final stop before the train station or the airport, which has daily flights to Stockholm.

Born in 1917 in Köpmanholmen, the small port where the Ulvön ferry departs, ceramic artist Hans Hedberg nevertheless spent his artistic career in France. The Hans Hedberg Museum in Örnsköldsvik displays what made him famous: giant ceramic fruits and eggs in vivid colors. Hedberg had his studio in Biot, in southern France, from 1949 onward. The museum is open on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 21 Strandgatan, and admission is free. On a Saturday or Sunday, stick to the viewpoint.

seo.h1_title: High Coast in 3 Days: Skuleberget, Ulvön, and Högbonden
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary explores Sweden’s High Coast, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000 because the land is still rising following the melting of the ice. You cross Högakustenbron, walk across the rock slabs at Rotsidan, and spend the night in the fishing village of Bönhamn. Next come Högbonden lighthouse, the summit of Skuleberget, and a night on the island of Ulvön, before Örnsköldsvik.
seo.seo_hook: Högakustenbron, Högbonden lighthouse, the summit of Skuleberget, and the island of Ulvön: 3 days on the High Coast, where the land is still rising by 8 mm a year.
featured_list: Högakustenbron: a 1,867 m bridge opened in 1997
Mannaminne: more than 50 buildings brought together by artist Anders Åberg
Högbonden: a lighthouse whose light shines 75 m above the sea
Skuleberget: a 295 m summit and Sweden’s first via ferrata
Ulvön: the fishing hamlet of Sandviken, rebuilt after the fire of 1786

itineraries.title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel up the Bohuslän coast from Marstrand to the Koster Islands via Smögen, Fjällbacka, and Tanum.
itineraries.notes: Marstrand is about 45 km from Gothenburg, and trains on the Bohusbanan line connect Strömstad to Gothenburg for the return trip. From September to May, several boat services and guided tours do not operate or run only on weekends: check schedules before setting out.
itineraries.climate: Plan your trip between late June and mid-August, when the Hållö boat service, guided tours of Carlsten, and Hållö Lighthouse operate daily. July is the warmest month, with average highs around 20 °C, and the sea reaches about 18 °C in July and August. Avoid October, the rainiest month, and bring a windbreaker even in summer.

visits.text: The most sweeping view of Marstrand takes some effort to reach: it is from Carlstens fästning, the fortress crowning the island’s highest point. King Charles X Gustav ordered construction to begin in 1658, the year the region became Swedish. It also served as a prison. Its most famous inmate, Lasse-Maja, was a thief who dressed as a woman to evade his pursuers. Sentenced to life in 1813, he was pardoned in 1839. The guided tour takes you through the kitchen where he worked. Admission: 120 Swedish kronor per adult in 2026, with guided tours in Swedish.

Glass-enclosed porches, carved wooden trim, and cobblestone streets: central Marstrand retains the look of a 19th-century seaside resort. In the 16th century, the island was one of Europe’s major herring fishing centers. When herring fishing declined, wealthy seaside vacationers sustained the island. King Oscar II was among these visitors. No cars travel on the island: wander the sloping lanes behind the waterfront, away from the bustle of the harbor.

Built between 1270 and 1319, Marstrands kyrka, Marstrand’s church, predates the fortress by more than three centuries. It probably served an order of Franciscan friars. The stone building was later expanded and remodeled several times, from 1690 to 1912. Its Baroque pulpit, carved in 1691, was given a simpler style in 1852. Opening hours vary: if the door is closed, walk around the medieval walls.

activities.text: If you arrive by car, leave it on Koön, the island opposite: cars are prohibited on Marstrandsön, the island with the fortress. The passenger ferry crosses the strait in about 2 minutes. During the day, it departs every 15 minutes; at night, it runs every 30 minutes on request. Buy your ticket on the Koön side, from the ticket machine or kiosk: it includes the return trip. Västtrafik single tickets for the region’s public transportation are not valid on board.

practical_info.tip: Without a car, take bus 302 from the Nils Ericson bus terminal at Gothenburg Central Station. It stops at Arvidsvik, 30 m from the ferry. On Koön, the parking lots closest to the ferry are the most expensive.

activities.text: Walk around Marstrandsön on the 5 km coastal trail, which the tourist office estimates takes 1 hour without stops. A detour leads to Nålsögat, “the eye of the needle,” a passage between two rocks so narrow that you have to squeeze through sideways. At the tip of the island, Skallens fyr, Skallen Lighthouse, marks the point where the Skagerrak and Kattegat meet, the two seas along Sweden’s west coast. The trail alternates between rocky stretches and stairs, and trail markers are sometimes missing: wear sturdy shoes.

practical_info.tip: Strandverket, along the route, has a swimming area for children. Allow 2 hours with stops for photos and swimming.

activities.text: “Kaja” is what Marstrand residents call strolling back and forth along the waterfront, often with an ice cream in hand. The tourist office describes the island’s harbor as Sweden’s largest marina. In early July, it hosts the GKSS Match Cup Sweden, a match racing regatta in which two sailboats compete head-to-head at a time. Come in the late afternoon, when the boats return to the harbor and the waterfront comes alive.

practical_info.tip: If you visit during the Match Cup in early July, book your accommodations well in advance.

visits.text: Smögenbryggan, the wooden boardwalk along Smögen’s harbor, stretches for nearly 800 meters, according to the tourist office. It is lined with sjöbodar, the sheds where fishermen once stored their gear, now converted into stores, cafés, and restaurants. Fishermen have sheltered in this harbor since the mid-16th century. In summer, it is Sweden’s busiest boardwalk: come early in the morning to see the boats without the crowds.

If you are up around 8 a.m. on a weekday, stop by the Smögens fiskauktion auction hall, Smögen’s fish auction. This is where boats unload their catch, and the public can still watch. The auction was founded in 1919 to help fishermen get a fair price. Today, it is Sweden’s second-largest fish auction. Sales take place online, with buyers from across Europe. Go on the morning of your departure, before heading to Fjällbacka.

First lit on November 1, 1842, Hållö Lighthouse is the oldest in Bohuslän, the coastal province explored on this trip. From Midsommar, the midsummer celebration in late June, through mid-August, the lighthouse and keeper’s house open daily, with guides on site. The house features exhibits on the island’s geology, flora, and fauna. Outside this period, book a guided tour by emailing the lighthouse.

Period furniture, household objects, and family photos: Fiskarstugan, the preserved fisherman’s cottage just above Smögenbryggan, shows how a Smögen family lived in the 19th century. It is maintained by the local history association, Smögens Hembygdsförening. Signs point the way from the boardwalk. The house opens only on certain summer days; during the rest of the year, visits must be requested through the association.

activities.text: Board the Hållöfärjan at Smögenbryggan: in 10 minutes, the boat takes you to Hållö, a granite island designated as a nature reserve. Its rock slabs were polished by ice during the last ice age. Near Slättehälla, a glacial pothole reaches four meters deep. This round hole was carved into the rock at the end of the ice age by meltwater flowing beneath the ice, carrying sand and gravel. In summer, the boat departs every 30 minutes, from morning until late afternoon.

practical_info.tip: The Hållöfärjan runs on a fixed schedule only in summer; in spring and fall, it is available only for charter on request. Bring water and a picnic.

activities.text: The day’s most beautiful swimming spot is Marmorbassängen, “the marble pool,” a hollow among smooth rocks on the island of Hållö. A ladder leads down into clear water with turquoise hues. The tourist office ranks Hållö’s waters among the saltiest in Sweden. The saltier the water, the more buoyant you are: you will float more easily here than in fresh water. The sea stays cool even in summer, so ease into the water gradually.

practical_info.tip: Avoid swimming in strong winds, when waves crash against the rocks.

activities.text: “Räkmacka” is the Swedish name for an open-faced shrimp sandwich: a slice of bread covered with peeled shrimp. According to the tourist office, it may have originated in Smögen in the early 1930s, at a restaurant by the harbor. Smögen even calls itself “the seafood capital.” Try one on an outdoor patio overlooking the fishing boats. In the off-season, check opening dates: some restaurants do not reopen until April.

practical_info.tip: The fish markets near the fish auction sell fish landed at the harbor.

visits.text: Huge boulders wedged above your head form a stone roof: Kungsklyftan is a roughly 200-meter-long cleft that splits Vetteberget hill in Fjällbacka in two. Its name means “the king’s cleft.” It commemorates King Oscar II’s visit in 1887, when he left his signature on the rock face at the northern entrance. Scenes from the film adaptation of Astrid Lindgren’s novel Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter were filmed here. The passage is steep, so wear closed-toe shoes.

Despite its small size, the fishing village of Fjällbacka attracted a Hollywood star. Starting in 1958, actress Ingrid Bergman spent every summer on Dannholmen, a nearby islet. After her death in 1982, her ashes were scattered around the island, and a bust of her was later unveiled in the village. The central square, Ingrid Bergmans torg, bears her name. Novelist Camilla Läckberg, who was born in Fjällbacka, sets several of her crime novels here: start at the square to recognize their settings.

In the mid-18th century, herring brought prosperity to Fjällbacka. Around 1850, the village was the busiest fishing port in its region. According to the tourist office, Swedish ansjovis originated at a cannery in Fjällbacka. Despite its name, it is made with sprats, small relatives of herring, rather than anchovies, and cured in brine for several months. Walk along the quay: you can explore the old village, squeezed between the hill and the sea, in 30 minutes.

activities.text: Climb the Vetteberget stairs from Ingrid Bergmans torg: at 74 meters, the hill towers over Fjällbacka. From the summit, views stretch across the harbor, the archipelago’s islands, and the inland countryside. The Vettebergsleden loop trail, marked in blue, is 4 km long and also passes through Kungsklyftan. It is steep in places, but numerous steps make the climb easier. At the trailhead, a QR code provides access to an audio guide to the trail.

practical_info.tip: Save the climb for clear skies: visibility is best in clear weather.

visits.text: Take time to study the Vitlycke rock panel, the most visited of the Tanum rock carvings, which were UNESCO-listed in 1994. Nearly 300 figures were pecked into this rock surface, about 22 meters high, by repeatedly striking the stone. They include ships, people, animals, and a bridal couple, the best-known carving in Bohuslän. The oldest date to around 1800 BCE. Never walk on the rock: it is fragile.

Vitlycke Museum, a few hundred meters from the rock panel, is the visitor center for the listed site. Inside, Bronze Age figures have been reconstructed based on excavations of graves and settlements. Outside, a reconstructed farm has two longhouses and a workshop. In summer, crafts from the period are practiced here. The museum is most active during the warmer months, and its hours vary by month: check its website before visiting. Admission is free for visitors under 20.

About 2 km from the museum, the Litsleby rock panel is nicknamed “the panel of the spear god.” A giant brandishing a spear towers over the other figures. The tourist office describes it as Scandinavia’s largest carved human figure. A wheelchair-accessible ramp lets you get close and take photographs without stepping onto the rock. A tactile panel also describes it through touch.

Musicians, dancers, warriors, hunters, deer, and dogs crowd the Fossum rock panel, about 4 km from the museum. Ships frame the densely packed scenes. They may tell a story of gods and goddesses. You can also spot a female figure known as the Fossum woman. About 100 meters to the east, the Balken carving shows a horse pulling the sun: take the detour on foot.

activities.text: If you have another hour, follow the Aspeberget trail, about 800 meters from the museum: a route just under a kilometer long links its carved rock panels. The three largest are painted red to help visitors make out the lines. This practice is criticized because it changes the rock’s original appearance. The very fragile bull panel remains covered for most of the year. Unpainted carvings are easier to make out early in the morning or late in the day, when low-angle light highlights their grooves.

practical_info.tip: The bull panel is uncovered for only a few months in summer: ask at the museum before heading up.

visits.text: Strömstads kyrka, the stone church in the town center, was built in 1768 and 1769. Following a fire, it was restored between 1817 and 1822, when its bell tower was added. Inside, model ships hang from the ceiling near gilded chandeliers and brass lamps. Look up as you enter. The church is open to visitors, and concerts are held here in summer.

activities.text: Drop off your bags in Strömstad, then follow Strandpromenaden, the waterfront promenade that runs alongside Laholmsparken park and Oscarsplatsen square. The town is one of Sweden’s oldest spa resorts. As early as 1782, visitors came to drink water from the Lejonkällan spring, which was believed to treat rheumatism. For a simple dinner, the tourist office suggests buying a bag of fresh shrimp and eating them on a dock in the marina.

practical_info.tip: Strömstad’s train station is in the center, within walking distance of the promenade and harbor.

activities.text: According to the tourist office, Korpeberget offers the best view over Strömstad’s rooftops. The name of this rocky hill means “raven mountain.” From the top, the town appears nestled between its sheltered bay and wooded hills. Head up late in the evening: in June and July, the sun sets late at this latitude, and the light lingers.

practical_info.tip: Bring a flashlight if you will be heading down late in the evening in late summer.

activities.text: Boats to the Koster Islands leave year-round from Norra hamnen, the northern harbor, in the heart of Strömstad. The crossing takes about 45 minutes, depending on your chosen stop. Get off at Ekenäs on Sydkoster, home to the national park’s visitor center. During peak summer 2026, from June 26 to August 2, the first departure was at 6:25 a.m., with boats running throughout the day. Pay on board by card, with no cash accepted, or through the Västtrafik To Go app.

practical_info.tip: The route changed operators in late September 2026: check the Västtrafik website for current schedules. In summer, space for bicycles on board is limited: rent one on Sydkoster instead.

visits.text: Naturum Kosterhavet, the national park’s visitor center, stands beside the Ekenäs dock on Sydkoster. Established in 2009, Kosterhavet is Sweden’s first marine national park. More than 6,000 marine species have been recorded here, including around 200 found nowhere else in Swedish waters. Many live in the 247-meter-deep Kosterfjord trench, where the water stays cold and salty. Admission is free: dip your hands into the touch tank to feel some of the park’s inhabitants.

A staircase, a cairn, and the entire archipelago spread out before you: Valfjäll is Sydkoster’s highest hill. Its cairn, a pile of stones built at the summit, is a familiar landmark for sailors. Benches and an orientation table help you identify Nordkoster and the neighboring islands. Leave your bike near Kosters kyrka, the small church east of the hill, before climbing up.

Opened in 1939, Kosters kyrka is Sweden’s westernmost place of worship. This small church is tucked into a valley in northern Sydkoster, between the Långegärde dock and the village square. It was designed in a restrained classical style by Knut Nordenskjöld, architect to the royal court. It is open to visitors only in summer; during the rest of the year, you can only view the exterior.

activities.text: If the water beckons, walk ten minutes from the Ekenäs dock to Rörvik, where a snorkeling trail begins. Snorkeling means swimming with a mask and snorkel. The route is about 200 meters long, in water 1 to 1.5 meters deep. A blue line along the bottom leads to eight signs introducing the local animals and plants. Never swim alone, or ask someone to watch you from shore.

practical_info.tip: Ask at Naturum Kosterhavet about equipment and the best time to go before entering the water.

activities.text: Rent a bike at the Ekenäs dock and ride across Sydkoster, where private cars are prohibited. Gravel paths connect the island’s three docks: Ekenäs, Långegärde, about 3.5 km away, and Kilesand, about 7 km away. You can return your bike at a different dock from the one where you rented it. Cycling is prohibited on hiking trails. For a barbecue, use only designated sites, bring your own wood or charcoal, and never use a disposable grill.

practical_info.tip: The rental service is staffed in summer; in the off-season, pay online or through Swish, the Swedish mobile payment app.

activities.text: Being too high can be a problem for a lighthouse. On Högen, the highest point in the Koster Islands, the old lighthouse stood so high that fog often hid its light from sailors. In 1891, it was replaced by Ursholmen’s two towers on an islet farther offshore. To climb Högen, cross the Kostersundet strait on the small yellow cable-operated passenger ferry, then follow Nordkoster’s marked trails. The yellow trail loops around the north of the island for 5.3 km, a walk of about two hours.

practical_info.tip: In peak season, the yellow passenger ferry has a crew member on board and accepts payment by card or Swish, but not cash. The boat to Strömstad also departs from Västra bryggan, Nordkoster’s western dock: note the last departure time before setting off on your walk.

seo.h1_title: Bohuslän in 4 Days: Marstrand, Smögen, Tanum, and Koster
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip follows the Bohuslän coast north from the car-free island of Marstrand to the Koster Islands, near the Norwegian border. Along the way, you visit Smögen’s harbor, the Kungsklyftan cleft in Fjällbacka, and Tanum’s UNESCO-listed Bronze Age rock carvings. The trip ends in Strömstad, where the train takes you back to Gothenburg.

itineraries.title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö
itineraries.subtitle: In 2 days, explore Gothenburg’s canals, Haga, Liseberg, and the island of Styrsö on foot, by tram, and by boat.
itineraries.notes: Paddan boats operate from late March to early November, and Liseberg opens from April to December. Outside these periods, walk along the canals and allow more time for museums. The art museum is due to close in 2028 for an expansion, with reopening planned for 2032.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to September, with highs of 17 to 23 °C, ideal for boat trips and island visits. From November to February, highs stay between 3 and 7 °C and rain is frequent: bring a raincoat and closed-toe shoes. October is the wettest month, with around 100 mm of rain.

visits.text: Coffee, spices, cheese: at Stora Saluhallen, Gothenburg’s large covered market, your nose is your first guide. The building dates from 1888–1889. Look up: iron arches support the glass roof. Around forty shops, bars, and small food counters line the aisles. Come on Saturday as early as 10 a.m. for coffee and a pastry before your boat trip, as the market is closed on Sundays.

visits.text: In 1621, King Gustavus Adolphus founded Gothenburg on marshy ground. Kungsportsplatsen, “King’s Gate Square,” takes its name from the main entrance through the old city walls. To build on this soft ground, the city called in Dutch engineers experienced in draining marshes. Gothenburg’s layout, with its canals, therefore follows the model of towns in Holland. The wide canal passing beneath the bridge at the square is Vallgraven, the former moat around the city walls.

activities.text: At Kungsportsplatsen, you’ll board a Paddan, an open-top boat that has been taking visitors through the canals since the 1930s. The tour lasts 50 minutes and passes under around twenty bridges, some of them very low. The boat follows Vallgraven, passing the opera house and the Feskekôrka fish market. It then heads into the harbor, passing below Läppstiftet, “the lipstick,” a tower nicknamed for its red and white stripes. The guide provides commentary in Swedish and English. All seating is outdoors: bring a jacket, even in summer.

practical_info.tip: Season: late March to early November, with daily departures from late April to late September. Tickets from 279 SEK. In winter, the Julpaddan (Christmas Paddan) travels along the canals to Liseberg from Friday to Sunday, November 27 to December 20, 2026.

to_next_leg.road_type: Along Vallgraven, the former moat around the city walls
to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops downtown; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or zero distance), whereas the stated walk of 1 km in 15 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Gothenburg locals call it Feskekôrka, “the fish church” in the local dialect. The nickname comes from the shape of the building, which opened in 1874: with its tall, pointed windows, it looks like a church. It is, however, Gothenburg’s fish market. After four years of restoration, it reopened in May 2024 with fishmongers’ counters, lunch deals, and two restaurants upstairs. Come at noon and eat overlooking the canal on one of the city’s largest terraces.

to_next_leg.justification: A walk between two nearby stops downtown; the routing engine calculated a driving route (due to one-way streets, a detour, or zero distance), whereas the stated walk of 0.4 km in 6 minutes is correct.

visits.text: Haga is a neighborhood that makes you want to slow down, with its small shops, antique dealers, and cafés. Queen Christina had it laid out in the mid-17th century as Gothenburg’s first suburb, home to sailors and dockworkers. On Haga Nygata, the main pedestrian street, the buildings have a stone ground floor and two wooden stories above. These workers’ apartment buildings, known as landshövdingehus, complied with fire regulations that prohibited more than two wooden stories. During Advent, the four weeks before Christmas, the street becomes a Christmas market on weekends.

activities.text: If you try just one thing in Haga, order a hagabulle at Café Husaren, at 28 Haga Nygata. It’s a giant cinnamon bun that Gothenburg’s tourist office describes as probably the largest in the world. In Sweden, this coffee break with a pastry is called fika. One bun is easily enough for two to share: ask for two cups.

practical_info.tip: If the line is long, other cafés line Haga Nygata, including Jacobs Café and Caféva, a vegetarian café open since 1983.

to_next_leg.road_type: Climb up the hill above Haga
to_next_leg.justification: Skansen Kronan overlooks Haga from the top of a hill reached by stairs: 400 m on foot in 10 minutes, including the climb, is the correct current figure; the driving route went around the hill.

visits.text: Despite being armed with 23 cannons, Skansen Kronan was never attacked. This small fort, whose name means “the Crown Fort,” was built between 1687 and 1700 on the hill overlooking Haga. It was intended to protect the city from a Danish attack. It later served as a prison, emergency housing, and then a military museum. Today, the interior is rented out for parties and conferences and is not open for casual visits. Head up for the view over Haga’s rooftops and downtown, especially beautiful late in the day.

visits.text: Göteborgs naturhistoriska museum, the city's natural history museum, stands on a hill in Slottsskogen. Its star attraction is a young blue whale nearly 16 meters long that washed ashore near Gothenburg in 1865. Its skin was stretched over a wooden frame. The West Sweden tourist board describes it as the world's only taxidermied blue whale on display. Visitors once entered its belly, which was fitted with benches. Today, its jaw opens only on special occasions, such as election days. Admission is 70 SEK, free for visitors under 20; closed Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot along the paths of Slottsskogen
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet urbain fait à pied entre goteborgs naturhistoriska museum et slottsskogen, environ 1000 m de marche réelle comptés 1 km : l'ancienne durée de 3 min venait du calcul voiture, elle est remplacée par 12 min de marche.

activities.text: You will then head back down into Slottsskogen, “the castle forest,” a wooded park covering 137 hectares, or nearly 190 soccer fields. Its name recalls how, when Gothenburg was founded, these woods belonged to an old fortress, Älvsborg. The zoo, free and open year-round, features Swedish animals: moose, ponies, and Gotland sheep. A pool is also home to seals and penguins. Allow 1 hour to walk around it.

practical_info.tip: Pony rides and the children's petting zoo (Barnens Zoo) operate from April through September. The Linnéplatsen tram stop is on the edge of the park, near the natural history museum.

activities.text: Even if you are not a thrill seeker, Liseberg is worth an evening visit. This amusement park opened in 1923 for the exhibition celebrating Gothenburg's 300th anniversary. Thrill seekers can ride Balder, a wooden roller coaster voted the world's best in its category in 2003 and 2005 in a major international poll. Others come for the atmosphere: at Christmas, more than five million light bulbs illuminate the walkways and market. You can sip glögg, Swedish mulled wine. If you do not go on any rides, a basic admission ticket is all you need.

practical_info.tip: The park opens from April through December. The 2026 Christmas season runs from November 14 to December 30, on select days only. Online Christmas prices: admission from 125 SEK, ride pass 235 SEK.

to_next_leg.road_type: Tram to Saltholmen, then ferry 281 or 282

visits.text: Tången, Styrsö's old fishing village, has white wooden houses clustered along narrow lanes. It also has a ferry dock: if you arrived at Bratten, to the east, you can leave from here after walking across the island. Along the way, the church dating from 1752 stands in Byn (“the village”), the island's oldest hamlet. West of Tången, the bays of Sandvik and Uttervik form a sheltered inlet where the water warms quickly in the sun. Save it for a summer swim.

activities.text: You will take the tram to the port of Saltholmen, then a ferry to Styrsö, a car-free island in the southern archipelago. Its roughly 1,400 residents get around on foot, by bike, by golf cart, or on mopeds fitted with cargo platforms. From the Bratten dock, climb to Stora Rös, the island's highest point. At the summit is a Bronze Age cairn, a pile of stones raised over a grave. The view stretches across the archipelago and the harbor entrance. A single Västtrafik Zone A ticket covers both the tram and the ferry.

practical_info.tip: Take tram 11 to Saltholmen, about 35 minutes from the city center, then ferry 281 or 282 to Styrsö Bratten, about 20 minutes. Ferries leave roughly once an hour: check the schedules in the Västtrafik app.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry to Saltholmen, then tram toward Götaplatsen

visits.text: In 1923, Gothenburg celebrated its 300th anniversary, and Göteborgs konstmuseum, the city's art museum, was completed for the occasion. It stands at the top of the main avenue, with a facade of yellow brick known as “Gothenburg brick.” Inside, the Fürstenberg Gallery, named after a couple who donated to the museum, brings together Nordic painters from the late 19th century, from Carl Larsson to Edvard Munch. The collection also ranges from Rembrandt to Picasso, including Van Gogh and Monet. On weekends, it is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 75 SEK, free for visitors under 20.

If you take just one photo at Götaplatsen, make it Poseidon, Carl Milles's fountain statue in the center of the square. Unveiled in 1931, it has become one of Gothenburg's symbols. Around it stand the art museum, the city theater, and the concert hall, where the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra performs. The best vantage point is at the top of the museum steps, with Kungsportsavenyen in the background.

visits.text: Humid heat and bird calls: Universeum's tropical rainforest transports you to another world within a few steps. This science center, which opened next to Liseberg in 2001, houses sloths, monkeys, and tropical birds in a large hall. Farther on, a 1.4-million-liter tank, more than half the capacity of an Olympic swimming pool, is home to sharks and tropical fish. A touch pool lets you touch rays. The other floors explore the human body, chemistry, and space through hands-on experiments. Buy your ticket online: it costs 30 SEK less than at the ticket counter.

seo.h1_title: Gothenburg in 2 Days: Haga, Canals, Liseberg, and Styrsö
seo.intro_paragraph: This 2-day weekend in Gothenburg is car-free, with travel on foot, by tram, and by boat. The first day follows the canals on a Paddan tour, takes in Feskekôrka, Haga, and Slottsskogen, and ends with an evening at Liseberg. The second day heads to the island of Styrsö in the southern archipelago before visiting the art museum and Universeum.
